# e1 — Vector Search with pgvector (build plan)

Source of truth: `research/V-pgvector.md` (pgvector README, CHANGELOG, source; 0.8.7 in PGlite). Blog errors from its
Contradictions section are avoided (`<=>` is a distance, not a similarity; index limits differ per type; Jaccard is for bit).

Shared dataset (`_kit.tsx` `ITEMS_SETUP`, ~0.3 s): `items` 10 000 × vector(32), 40 clustered topics (centre ± U(-0.5,0.5)),
`region = topic % 4`, `category` random 0–9; `queries` (20), `truth` (exact top-10, built before any index), view `recall`.
Single INSERT…SELECT…GROUP BY generator (no correlated subqueries). Clustered, because uniform data gives misleading recall.
Lesson 6 uses `docs` 2 000 × vector(256) (~1 s) so binary quantization is meaningful.
HNSW level assignment and IVFFlat k-means sampling are random, so measured recall varies in the 2nd–3rd decimal between builds; text says "about".

text:
# E2 — Time-Series with TimescaleDB (plan)

Facts come from `research/W-timescaledb.md` (TimescaleDB 2.32.0 README, changelog, official docs) and the PostgreSQL 18
docs. TimescaleDB cannot run in PGlite: visualizers simulate it, playgrounds run the native PostgreSQL 18 equivalent,
production examples and pitfalls show real 2.32-era TimescaleDB SQL. Every playground number below was measured on
PGlite (PostgreSQL 18.6) with the exact lesson SQL.

Editions, stated in every lesson where relevant: **Apache 2 edition** (`timescaledb.license = 'apache'`; what Neon ships:
"Only Apache-2 licensed features are supported. Compression is not supported.") has hypertables, `show_chunks`,
`drop_chunks`, `add_dimension`, `time_bucket`, `first`, `last`, `histogram`. **Community edition** (Tiger Data License,
default `timescale`) adds the columnstore, continuous aggregates, retention policies, jobs (`add_job`),
`time_bucket_gapfill`/`locf`/`interpolate`, SkipScan. Tiering to object storage is Tiger Cloud only.

---

title: 1. time-series-basics — Time-series data on PostgreSQL
text:
Facts
1. Time-series rows arrive in time order, are rarely updated, are queried by time range and age out.
2. Rows inserted in time order make the heap physically sorted: `pg_stats.correlation` = 1 for `time` (brin.html, view-pg-stats.html).
3. BRIN stores min/max per block range (`pages_per_range`, default 128) (brin.html).
4. Measured: 200,000 rows (1/s) → heap 1274 pages / 10192 kB, 157 rows per page; BRIN (32 pages/range) 24 kB; B-tree 4408 kB.
5. A 1-hour query on BRIN: `Heap Blocks: lossy=32`, `Rows Removed by Index Recheck: 1424`, 3600 rows (one 32-page range).
6. Shuffled copy: correlation ≈ 0, the same query reads `lossy=1280` blocks and rechecks away 196,400 rows.
7. `date_bin(stride, ts, origin)` buckets timestamps (functions-datetime.html); no months; origin required.
8. Declarative partitioning gives chunk-like pruning and cheap retention, but no automatic partition creation (ddl-partitioning.html).
9. TimescaleDB is an extension that must be in `shared_preload_libraries`; current 2.32.0 supports PG 16–18.
10. Editions and Neon limits.
Visualizer: BRIN range map of the real 200k-row table (40 ranges × 32 pages). Drag the query window; the ranges whose min/max
overlap light up; stats tiles show lossy pages, rows rechecked, rows returned. Toggle "time-ordered" vs "shuffled".
Second panel: edition matrix (Apache / Community / Neon) lighting features.
Playground: `readings` 200k rows + BRIN. Presets: physical order & correlation; BRIN plan; B-tree vs BRIN size; hourly
`date_bin`; shuffled table; latest reading per sensor.
Production: IoT platform keeping 30 days of 1 Hz readings in a plain table; BRIN + daily partitions vs moving to TimescaleDB.
Pitfalls: BRIN on non-correlated column; DELETE-based retention bloat; `date_bin` month error; assuming Neon has compression.

title: 2. hypertables-chunks — Hypertables and chunks
text:
Facts: `CREATE TABLE … WITH (tsdb.hypertable, tsdb.partition_column, tsdb.chunk_interval)` since 2.20 (auto partition
column 2.23); default chunk interval 7 days; `create_hypertable(rel, by_range('time', INTERVAL '1 day'))`; chunks in
`_timescaledb_internal._hyper_<ht>_<chunk>_chunk`, created on demand; boundaries aligned from epoch 0;
`set_chunk_time_interval` affects only new chunks; sizing rule: indexes of active chunks within 25% of memory (64 GB:
2 GB/day → 7 days, 10 GB/day → 1 day); >1000 chunks is a warning sign; default index `time DESC`; UNIQUE must include the
time column; `add_dimension(by_hash)` multiplies chunks and is discouraged; ChunkAppend runtime exclusion.
Visualizer: live hypertable simulation. Buttons: ingest 6 h, late row, far-future row; Segmented chunk interval
(6 h / 1 day / 7 days) and hash partitions (1 / 2); drag a query window to see chunk exclusion; mode toggle TimescaleDB vs
native partitioning (ERROR no partition). Sizing calculator.
Playground: native partitioned `conditions` with an `ensure_chunk()` helper. Presets: chunk list; plan-time exclusion;
runtime exclusion (`Subplans Removed: 5`); no automatic chunk (`try_sql`), then ensure_chunk; unique key rule;
hash sub-partitioning; ordered append vs Merge Append.

title: 3. time-bucket-gapfill — time_bucket and gap filling
text:
Facts: `time_bucket(width, ts [, offset] [, origin] [, timezone])` returns bucket start; default origin 2000-01-03 (Monday)
below 1 month, 2000-01-01 for months; UTC alignment; timezone argument; `date_bin` equivalent but no months;
`time_bucket_gapfill` needs WHERE bounds, top-level only, Community; `locf`, `interpolate` Community; `first/last` Apache,
not index-assisted on rowstore; PG 18 has no `IGNORE NULLS`; `time_bucket_ng` removed 2.25.
Visualizer: mode "Bucketing" (72 h axis across the 2026-03-29 Berlin DST switch; width, origin, offset, timezone controls;
readings snap into buckets) and mode "Gap filling" (hourly bars 11, –, 20, –, –, 50; toggle plain / gapfill / locf /
interpolate → 11 15.5 20 30 40 50).
Playground: `metrics` sparse rows. Presets: date_bin = time_bucket; months; DST; gapfill; locf; interpolate; first/last.

title: 4. continuous-aggregates — Continuous aggregates
5. compression-columnstore — Compression and the columnstore
text:
Facts: Hypercore = rowstore + columnstore (renamed from compression in 2.18); up to 1000 rows per batch per segmentby value;
per-batch min/max metadata; codecs (delta-of-delta + simple-8b + RLE before 2.32, AIC default in 2.32, Gorilla XOR floats,
dictionary); settings `segmentby`, `orderby`; policy `add_columnstore_policy(after =>)`; default schedule is documented
two ways (contradiction — never one number); DML decompresses only affected batches,
`max_tuples_decompressed_per_dml_transaction` 100000; "90%+" typical, demo 194 MB → 24 MB; Community only.
Visualizer: Stepper of 12 rows → segment → order → batch arrays → codecs → batch skipping → UPDATE decompresses one batch;
Segmented segmentby (device / none / reading_id).
Playground: `ticks` 30k rows: 1568 kB rowstore vs 216 kB arrays (30 batches); skipping; delta-of-delta; segmentby choices
(unique segmentby 4104 kB); updating one value rewrites the batch.

title: 6. retention-jobs — Retention, tiering and jobs
text:
Facts: `drop_chunks` drops whole chunks only; `add_retention_policy(drop_after)` one per hypertable; jobs scheduler,
`timescaledb_information.jobs/job_stats`; `add_job(proc, schedule_interval, config)`, `fixed_schedule` default true;
failure backoff; `max_background_workers` 16; cagg + retention interaction; tiering Tiger Cloud only; multi-node removed in 2.14.
Visualizer: lifecycle timeline (daily chunks, now advancing): rowstore → columnstore → tiered → dropped; sliders for
`drop_after`, columnstore `after`, cagg `start_offset`; warning when retention cuts into the refresh window; jobs table.
Playground: 10 daily partitions; DELETE WAL vs drop job; jobs registry + `run_due_jobs()` emulating the scheduler; failure backoff.

section: 7. hyperfunctions — Hyperfunctions: time-weighted averages, candlesticks, percentiles and counters
title: 7. hyperfunctions — Hyperfunctions: time-weighted averages, candlesticks, percentiles and counters
text:
Facts): extension `timescaledb_toolkit` 1.27.0 (2026-11-05), PG 16–18, trusted since 1.23, Timescale
License (Community edition), pre-installed on Tiger Cloud and in `timescaledb-ha`, packages per PG version, not on Neon; two-step
aggregation (aggregate → summary → accessor, `rollup`); `time_weight('LOCF'|'linear', ts, v)` + `average`/`integral`/
`interpolated_average`; `average` of one point is NULL; `candlestick_agg(ts, price, volume)` + open/high/low/close/volume/vwap;
`percentile_agg` = `uddsketch(200, 0.001, v)`, `approx_percentile(p, s)`, `approx_percentile_rank(v, s)`, key ⌈log_γ x⌉, merge = add
counts; `counter_agg(ts, v [, bounds])`: decrease = reset, `delta`, `rate`, `extrapolated_rate(s, 'prometheus')` needs bounds,
`num_resets`, `interpolated_delta`; `stats_agg`, `heartbeat_agg`; `toolkit_experimental` objects are dropped on extension update.
Visualizer: four simulated modes (Segmented). Time-weighted: 8 irregular samples revealed step by step, shaded LOCF/linear area,
stats naive vs TWA, bucket view average vs interpolated_average. Candlestick: 8 ticks build two 1-minute candles, then rollup to
2 minutes. Percentiles: three hourly UddSketches (α = 0.05) as log-bucket histograms, merged by adding counts; avg of p95s vs merged
p95 vs exact. Counter: raw sawtooth with two resets, corrected cumulative line, per-bucket deltas vs rollup.
Playground (native PG 18): readings / ticks / requests / scrapes. Presets: naive vs LOCF/linear via lead(); buckets, interpolation
and summary rollup; OHLC with array_agg + rollup of partial state; exact percentiles and avg-of-p95; mergeable log-bucket sketch;
counter resets via lag()+CASE and the boundary increase.
Production: API platform storing percentile_agg + counter_agg in an hourly cagg, daily via rollup.
Pitfalls: averaging irregular samples; averaging percentiles; ignoring counter resets (and summing bucket deltas); experimental
functions dropped/renamed on upgrade.

# E3 — Distributed PostgreSQL (plan)

Track: ecosystem. Folder `app/src/lessons/e3/`. Shared helpers: `_ui.tsx` (buttons, stats, `hashint4` port verified
against PGlite on 2053 values, `TRY_SQL` setup snippet). Facts below come from
`research/X-distributed-postgres.md` (primary docs: Citus 14, YugabyteDB, Spock 5, PGD 6.5, Patroni, Neon, Aurora) and the
PG 18 docs. The playground never pretends an extension is installed: it runs native PG 18 stand-ins on one node and says so.

Global playground rules: no statement may wait on a lock (lock_timeout does not fire in the browser). Prepared
transactions are always resolved in the same preset; locked rows are probed only with `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` (inside
`try_sql`) or `SKIP LOCKED`. No `CREATE SUBSCRIPTION`, no logical decoding.

---

section: 1. why-distribute — Why and how to distribute PostgreSQL
title: 1. why-distribute — Why and how to distribute PostgreSQL
text:
Key facts
1. PostgreSQL is single-node: one data directory, one WAL stream; it ships replication and FDWs but no sharding, no distributed txn manager, no automatic failover (different-replication-solutions, warm-standby-failover).
2. Three mechanisms: replication (copies), distribution (parts), decentralization (storage vs compute).
3. The protocol is synchronous: 20 ms per transaction = 50 txn/s per session (computed: 1000/20).
4. Read replicas: writes on one primary; reads scale; no read-your-writes / monotonic reads when async (high-availability).
5. Shared storage: Aurora 10 GB protection groups, 6 copies across 3 AZs, write quorum 4 of 6, up to 15 replicas; Neon compute → safekeepers (Paxos quorum) → pageserver → object storage.
6. Sharding (Citus): coordinator + workers, hash by distribution column, 32 shards default.
7. Distributed SQL (YugabyteDB): tablets, Raft per tablet, a leader per tablet, re-election in about 2 s.
8. Multi-master (PGD, Spock): every node writable, async logical replication, conflicts resolved after commit.
9. CAP: on a partition choose consistency or availability; Raft/Paxos systems are CP, async multi-master is AP.
10. PACELC: else latency vs consistency; `synchronous_commit` levels and `synchronous_standby_names` FIRST/ANY are that knob (runtime-config-replication, warm-standby).
Visualizer: architecture explorer. Segmented over 5 architectures; one SVG with client, nodes and storage; buttons
"Send a write" (viz-next), "Send a read", "Fail a node" (per architecture: primary / storage node / worker / tablet leader / one site).
Animated packets along hop paths; a fact panel (writes on, reads from, consistency, on failure, CAP). Second panel:
latency budget sliders (RTT, round trips per txn, sessions) → TPS per session and ceiling.
Playground: native building blocks. Presets: WAL stream bytes per write; commit knobs; a physical slot; hash partitions as shards; a publication; latency maths in SQL.
Production: a SaaS that wants "to go distributed" measures first and picks replicas + HA. Pitfalls: replica read-your-writes, single sync standby stalls commits, distributing before batching/pooling, "cluster" ambiguity.

title: 2. sharding-citus — Sharding with Citus
text:
Key facts: coordinator/workers, MX mode (Citus 11+); `create_distributed_table(table, column, colocate_with => 'default')`;
`citus.shard_count` 32; shard `<table>_<shardid>`; `pg_dist_shard` shardminvalue/shardmaxvalue over int32 hash tokens
(2^32/32 = 134,217,728 per shard); colocation by same type + shard count; reference tables (one shard on every worker,
2PC writes); schema-based sharding (12.0, `citus_schema_distribute`, ~1–10k tenants vs row-based ~1–1M+);
PK/UNIQUE must include the distribution column; FKs: colocated incl. dist column, or → reference; not reference → distributed;
changing the dist column type is refused. Sources: ddl-partitioning (stand-in), ddl-constraints.
Visualizer: shard map. 32 shards coloured by worker (2/3/4 workers), type a company id → hashint4 token → shard →
worker; tables companies/campaigns/ads colocated (same shard index, same worker) vs `colocate_with => 'none'`; reference
table copies on every worker; mode distributed / reference / schema-based. viz-next = "Route next key".
Playground: `pg_dist_shard_sim` built with hashint4; companies/campaigns/ads hash-partitioned 4 ways (colocated
stand-in); unique and FK rules via `try_sql`; schema-per-tenant.

title: 3. distributed-queries — Distributed query execution
text:
Key facts: router (fast path) when the filter pins the dist column; multi-shard = one task per shard, merged on the
coordinator; `Custom Scan (Citus Adaptive)`, `Task Count: 32`, `Tasks Shown: One of 32`; aggregates split
(avg → sum + count per shard); push-pull recursive planning with `read_intermediate_result`, `citus.max_intermediate_result_size` 1 GB;
repartition joins off by default (`citus.enable_repartition_joins`); `citus.max_adaptive_executor_pool_size` 16;
rebalancer `citus_rebalance_start()` (by_disk_size default, background), `get_rebalance_table_shards_plan()`,
`citus_move_shard_placement`, `shard_transfer_mode` auto/force_logical/block_writes; `isolate_tenant_to_new_shard`.
Visualizer: Stepper per query type (router / fan-out aggregate / colocated join / repartition join / rebalance), coordinator
+ 3 workers, tasks fly out, partial results fly back with real numbers from the stand-in data; EXPLAIN panel.
Playground: partition pruning, Append fan-out, Partial/Finalize aggregate and manual sum/count, partitionwise join,
non-colocated join, detach/attach and split (modulus 4 → 8).

title: 4. distributed-transactions — Distributed transactions and consistency
text:
Key facts: PREPARE TRANSACTION / COMMIT PREPARED / ROLLBACK PREPARED, GID < 200 bytes, `max_prepared_transactions` 0 disables,
prepared state on disk, any session can finish it, holds locks and xmin (sql-prepare-transaction, view-pg-prepared-xacts);
postgres_fdw has no 2PC (postgres-fdw); 2PC blocks when the coordinator dies after PREPARE; HLC = (physical, logical);
YugabyteDB intents + status tablet; isolation mapping; sequences per node; uniqueness/FKs across shards.
Visualizer: tabs: 2PC Stepper (commit / vote no / coordinator dies → in-doubt → recovery) with lanes and
pg_prepared_xacts; HLC lab (two clocks with skew, send/receive); "what changes" matrix.
Playground config: `max_prepared_transactions = 10`, `track_commit_timestamp = on`. Two schemas as two participants.

title: 5. distributed-sql-multimaster — Distributed SQL and multi-master
text:
Key facts: YugabyteDB YQL over DocDB (RocksDB), YB-TServer/YB-Master, tablets with Raft, hash 0x0000–0xFFFF, first PK column hashed,
`SPLIT INTO n TABLETS`; v2025.1 rebased on PG 15; RC only with `yb_enable_read_committed_isolation` (default for new
universes from v2025.2), wait queues default since v2024.1. PGD 6.5: commit scopes, conflict types and resolvers,
global sequences; Spock 5: `spock.conflict_resolution` error / apply_remote / keep_local / last_update_wins,
delta-apply, FKs not enforced during apply; PG 18 conflict types (`confl_*`) (logical-replication-conflicts).
Visualizer: tabs: Raft (3 nodes × 3 tablets, write → majority, fail/recover nodes, elections); conflict lab
(two nodes, overwrite or increment, skew slider, 5 resolution modes, converge/diverge/lost update).
Playground: two schemas as two nodes with commit timestamps, a trigger-built change log, LUW and delta resolution in SQL.

title: 6. ha-clusters — High-availability clusters in practice
text:
Key facts: Patroni leader key in a DCS (etcd/etcd3/Consul/ZooKeeper/Kubernetes); ttl 30 / loop_wait 10 / retry_timeout 10,
`loop_wait + 2*retry_timeout <= ttl`; `maximum_lag_on_failover`; REST `/primary` 200 only on the leader, `/replica`;
HAProxy `option httpchk`, `inter 3s fall 3 rise 2`; `synchronous_mode`; `pg_rewind`; STONITH (warm-standby-failover);
`pg_promote()`; sync replication `FIRST`/`ANY` (warm-standby).
Visualizer: Stepper generated from ttl/loop_wait/retry_timeout sliders; scenarios crash / partition (fencing) /
switchover; lanes for pg1–pg3, etcd leader key with TTL bar, HAProxy routes; rule check turns red on split-brain window.
Playground: role and lag queries, slots per member, per-transaction sync commit, settings contexts, timeline/WAL file, the timing rule in SQL.

# e4 — Spatial Data with PostGIS (build plan)

Source of truth: `research/Y-postgis.md` (PostGIS 3.6 manual + numbers measured on PostGIS 3.6.2 / GEOS 3.14 / PROJ 9.7 in PGlite).
Playground: `extensions: ['postgis']` in all four lessons. All data is invented and generated with `generate_series` (no random()).
Shared JS in `_kit.tsx`: deterministic hash, STR-packed R-tree (leaf fanout 6, inner fanout 4), box/point distance, Tile/Btn/Slider/Sql.

section: 1. spatial-basics — Geometry, geography and coordinate systems
title: 1. spatial-basics — Geometry, geography and coordinate systems
text:
Facts (using_postgis_dbmanagement, ST_Distance, ST_Transform, ST_MakePoint):
1. geometry = plane, Cartesian math, units of the SRID; geography = spheroid, metres, fewer functions.
2. geometry default SRID 0, geography default 4326; geography only accepts lon/lat SRSs.
3. Order is x = longitude, y = latitude.
4. ST_MakePoint has no SRID; ST_Point(x, y, srid) / ST_SetSRID add it; ST_SetSRID relabels, ST_Transform recomputes.
5. Typmod `geometry(Point,4326)` rejects wrong SRID and wrong type; registers in geometry_columns.
6. spatial_ref_sys: 8500 rows; srid, auth_name, auth_srid, srtext, proj4text.
7. London–Paris: 3.63 degrees (4326 geometry), 343.9 km geography, 537.3 km in 3857, 344.3 km in 3035.
8. 3857 inflates distances by about 1/cos(lat); 1°×1° cells shrink from 12 309 km² (equator) to 6 123 km² (60°).
9. Antimeridian: 359 degrees vs 111 km.
10. Formats: WKT, EWKT, HEXEWKB canonical output, GeoJSON (RFC 7946 = 4326).
Viz: graticule plane morphing between lon/lat and Web Mercator (motion path morph); four city pairs; distance read-outs per method;
"swap lat/lon" toggle shows the misplaced points and the wrong distance; latitude slider for the 1°×1° cell area.
Playground: `cities` (7 city coordinates typed in as points, not a map dataset) + a 1° grid, presets: SRIDs, three distances, area by latitude, typmod errors, formats, antimeridian.
Production: delivery app storing lat/lon in two float columns and measuring with 3857 → fix with geography column.
Pitfalls: swapped coordinates, degrees as metres, ST_SetSRID vs ST_Transform, 3857 for measurement.

section: 1. relational-basics — Tables, rows and your first query
title: 1. relational-basics — Tables, rows and your first query
text:
Facts
1. A relational database stores data in **tables**: named collections of **rows**; each row has the same named, typed **columns** (tutorial-concepts).
2. Rows in a table have no guaranteed order; order exists only with ORDER BY (tutorial-concepts, queries-order).
3. Hierarchy: a **cluster** (one server) holds databases; a database holds **schemas**; schemas hold tables; default schema `public` (manage-ag-overview, ddl-schemas).
4. Clients connect to exactly one database per connection; the server process runs SQL and returns rows (tutorial-arch).
5. `SELECT select_list FROM table`; `*` = all columns (tutorial-select, queries-select-lists).
6. Select-list items can be expressions: `price * 1.2` (tutorial-select).
7. `AS` renames an output column; `AS` is optional except before some keywords; an unnamed expression is called `?column?` (queries-select-lists; verified).
8. A table alias `FROM products p` lets you write `p.name` (queries-table-expressions).
9. `--` starts a line comment, `/* */` a block comment (sql-syntax-lexical).
10. A statement ends with `;`; keywords and unquoted names are case-insensitive (sql-syntax-lexical).
11. `numeric(8,2) * 1.2` gives `28.800`: the result scale is the sum of input scales (verified).
12. `current_database()`, `current_schema()`, `current_user` show where you are: `postgres`, `public`, `postgres` (functions-info; verified).
Visualizer: Stepper. Left: nested hierarchy cluster → database → schema → table (active level glows). Right: the products grid with
column/row highlighting, SQL card and animated result table. Steps: hierarchy, table anatomy (row vs column vs cell), `SELECT *`,
column list, expression + alias, table alias, comment and semicolon, client → server round trip. Click any cell to inspect it (row id, column, type, value).
Playground presets: SELECT *, pick columns, expressions with AS, where am I, list tables via information_schema, comments.
Production: an analyst's ad-hoc export uses an explicit column list instead of `SELECT *`.
Pitfalls: relying on row order without ORDER BY; `SELECT *` in application code; double quotes for strings; missing semicolon in psql.
Going deeper: I1 "What PostgreSQL is".

section: 2. create-and-insert — Creating tables and inserting rows
title: 2. create-and-insert — Creating tables and inserting rows
text:
Facts
1. `CREATE TABLE name (col type constraints, …)` (ddl-basics, sql-createtable).
2. Common types: `int` (4 bytes), `bigint` (8), `text`, `numeric(p,s)` exact, `boolean`, `date`, `timestamptz` (datatype-*).
3. `PRIMARY KEY` = unique + not null, creates an index (ddl-constraints).
4. `NOT NULL` rejects NULL: error 23502 with "Failing row contains" (verified).
5. `DEFAULT` used when a column is omitted or the keyword DEFAULT is written (ddl-default, dml-insert).
6. `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` auto-numbers; supplying a value errors 428C9 unless `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`; BY DEFAULT allows overrides (sql-createtable; verified).
7. Failed inserts still consume identity numbers: gaps (functions-sequence; verified id 4 skipped).
8. Multi-row `VALUES (…), (…)` in one statement (dml-insert).
9. `INSERT … SELECT` copies query results (dml-insert).
10. `RETURNING` returns the inserted rows, including generated ids (dml-returning).
11. Single quotes = string literal, double quotes = identifier; `''` escapes a quote; unquoted names fold to lower case (sql-syntax-lexical; verified `"Orders"` vs `orders`).
12. `DROP TABLE [IF EXISTS]` removes table and data (sql-droptable).
13. Bad input for a type errors 22P02 (`'maybe'` for boolean) (verified).
Visualizer: Stepper building `customers` live: CREATE draws header with type/constraint chips; inserts animate rows in, defaults
pulse, identity counter ticks; failing inserts shake red with real error text and burn an id; RETURNING panel.
Playground: create, insert one + RETURNING, multi-row, defaults, errors via a `try_sql` helper, INSERT … SELECT, quoting, DROP.
Production: signup service inserting and getting the id back in one round trip with RETURNING.
Pitfalls: supplying ids manually with identity; double quotes for strings; mixed-case quoted identifiers; float for money.
Going deeper: I2 "Primitive types, alignment and padding".

title: 3. filter-and-sort — Filtering and sorting
text:
Facts
1. WHERE keeps rows whose condition is **true**; false and NULL are both dropped (queries-table-expressions).
2. Comparison `= <> != < > <= >=` (functions-comparison).
3. Precedence: NOT > AND > OR; use parentheses (sql-syntax-lexical operator precedence).
4. `IN (list)`, `BETWEEN a AND b` inclusive both ends (functions-comparison).
5. `LIKE`: `%` any run, `_` one char; case-sensitive; `ILIKE` case-insensitive (PG extension) (functions-matching).
6. `x = NULL` is never true; use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` (functions-comparison; verified 0 rows).
7. Three-valued logic: NULL AND false = false, NULL OR true = true, NOT NULL = NULL (functions-logical).
8. `x NOT IN (…, NULL)` is never true (functions-subquery / comparisons).
9. ORDER BY multiple keys, ASC default, DESC; NULLs sort as larger: last in ASC, first in DESC; NULLS FIRST/LAST override (queries-order).
10. LIMIT n / OFFSET m; without ORDER BY the subset is unpredictable (queries-limit).
11. `FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES` also returns rows tying the last; needs ORDER BY (sql-select; verified 4 rows).
12. `DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows; NULLs count as equal for DISTINCT (queries-select-lists).
Visualizer: live filter lab. Choose a WHERE condition; each row shows its evaluated value (true/false/NULL chip); rows not true fade.
Then sort key/direction/NULLS and a LIMIT slider re-order with layout animations. Side panel: three-valued truth table (click an operator).
Playground: comparison, AND/OR precedence, IN/BETWEEN, LIKE/ILIKE, NULL traps, ORDER BY NULLS, LIMIT/OFFSET/WITH TIES, DISTINCT.
Production: "low stock" alert missing items whose stock is NULL.
Pitfalls: `= NULL`; OR without parentheses; NOT IN with NULL; LIMIT without ORDER BY.
Going deeper: I3 "Designing indexes".

title: 4. aggregate-basics — Counting, summing and grouping
text:
Facts
1. Aggregates compute one result from many rows: count, sum, avg, min, max (tutorial-agg, functions-aggregate).
2. `count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts non-NULL values (verified kitchen 3 vs 2).
3. All aggregates except count ignore NULL inputs and return NULL for zero rows (functions-aggregate).
4. GROUP BY forms one group per distinct key; every select-list column must be grouped or aggregated: error 42803 (queries-table-expressions; verified).
5. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after (tutorial-agg).
6. Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE (42803) (verified).
7. Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT (sql-select).
8. So ORDER BY may use an output alias, but WHERE and HAVING cannot (sql-select).
9. `avg(numeric)` returns many decimals; `round(x, 2)` for presentation (functions-math).
10. Group by an expression, such as `price >= 20` (queries-table-expressions).
11. NULL group keys form one group (queries-table-expressions).
Visualizer: pipeline Stepper over one query (WHERE price < 100, GROUP BY category, HAVING count(*) >= 3, ORDER BY avg DESC, LIMIT 1):
stage rail lights up; rows fade out at WHERE, fly into buckets at GROUP BY, buckets collapse to one row with aggregates, HAVING strikes office,
SELECT computes columns, ORDER BY swaps, LIMIT cuts. Result home | 3 | 33.00.
Playground: count(*) vs count(col), sum/avg/min/max, GROUP BY, the 42803 error, HAVING vs WHERE, group by expression, the pipeline query.
Production: daily sales summary per category for a dashboard.
Pitfalls: non-grouped column; count(col) where count(*) meant; aggregate in WHERE; sum of nothing is NULL.
Going deeper: F4 "Aggregates, FILTER and GROUPING SETS" and I3 "From SQL text to rows".

title: 5. change-data-safely — Updating and deleting safely
text:
Facts
1. `UPDATE t SET col = expr WHERE …` changes matching rows; without WHERE, every row (dml-update).
2. `DELETE FROM t WHERE …`; without WHERE, every row (dml-delete).
3. Command tag reports rows affected: `UPDATE 3`, `DELETE 1` (sql-update, sql-delete).
4. SET expressions see the old row values (`price = price * 1.1`) (sql-update).
5. `RETURNING` shows changed rows (dml-returning).
6. Outside BEGIN, each statement commits by itself (autocommit) (tutorial-transactions).
7. `BEGIN … COMMIT` makes a group atomic; `ROLLBACK` undoes everything since BEGIN (tutorial-transactions).
8. After an error inside a transaction, every statement fails (25P02) until ROLLBACK (tutorial-transactions; verified).
9. `TRUNCATE` empties a table fast, takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, fires no ON DELETE triggers, can `RESTART IDENTITY`; it is transaction-safe (sql-truncate).
10. DELETE leaves dead rows for VACUUM; TRUNCATE reclaims space immediately (sql-truncate, routine-vacuuming).
11. A SELECT with the same WHERE previews exactly the rows an UPDATE will touch (same snapshot logic for a single session).
Visualizer: two modes (safe workflow / missing WHERE). Steps: preview SELECT highlights rows; BEGIN; UPDATE … RETURNING changes cells
(old → new); check count; COMMIT (rows turn solid) or ROLLBACK (values spring back). Transaction badge and "what others see" lane.
Playground: preview, BEGIN/UPDATE/ROLLBACK, BEGIN/UPDATE/COMMIT, DELETE RETURNING, the missing WHERE caught by rollback, aborted transaction, TRUNCATE vs DELETE.
Production: a support engineer fixing a mispriced category with the preview → transaction → check → commit routine.
Pitfalls: missing WHERE; forgetting COMMIT leaves a transaction open; aborted transaction errors; TRUNCATE locks and skips triggers.
Going deeper: I4 "ACID and transactions" and F4 "INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE: what really happens".

# f2 — Working with Data (build plan)

Audience: beginners moving to intermediate. Every result below was run on PGlite (PostgreSQL 18.6, UTF8, TimeZone UTC by default).
Scratch scripts: `scratchpad/f2/*.sql`, `cap.mjs` (cast matrix, division table, 0.1 sums).

title: 1. text-functions — Text and strings
text:
Facts
1. `||` concatenates; one NULL makes the whole result NULL: `'a' || NULL` → NULL (functions-string).
2. `concat` ignores NULL args (`concat('a',NULL,'b')` → `ab`); `concat_ws(', ','Ann',NULL,'Lee')` → `Ann, Lee` (functions-string).
3. `||` accepts a non-string on one side: `'Value: ' || 42` (functions-string).
4. `length`/`char_length` count characters, `octet_length` counts bytes: `josé` 4 vs 5, `😀` 1 vs 4 (functions-string).
5. `lower/upper/initcap`: `initcap('hello wORLD o''neil')` → `Hello World O'Neil` (functions-string).
6. `trim` removes spaces by default; `ltrim('00123')` stays `00123`, `ltrim('00123','0')` → `123` (functions-string).
7. `substring(s FROM start FOR n)`, positions start at 1; `substring('PostgreSQL', 0, 3)` → `Po` (virtual position 0) (functions-string).
8. `position('SQL' IN 'PostgreSQL')` → 8; 0 when absent; `strpos` has the reverse argument order (functions-string).
9. `split_part(s, delim, n)`; negative n counts from the end (PG14+); past the end → empty string (functions-string).
10. `format()`: `%s` value, `%I` identifier (quoted if needed), `%L` literal (NULL → `NULL`) (functions-string).
11. Regex: `~` matches anywhere unless anchored, `~*` case-insensitive; `regexp_replace(..., 'g')` replaces all; `regexp_match` returns first match groups; `regexp_matches(...,'g')` returns one row per match and drops rows with none (functions-matching).
12. `LIKE` must match the whole string; `ILIKE` is case-insensitive (functions-matching).
13. `citext` compares case-insensitively; `UNIQUE` on citext rejects `Ann@x.com` vs `ann@X.COM` (citext).
14. Nondeterministic ICU collation (`deterministic = false`) makes `=` case-insensitive; ILIKE and regex are not supported with it (error), LIKE is (collation, functions-matching).
Visualizer: string workbench. Editable input (presets: padded name, email, accented text with emoji). Function picker. Input and output drawn as character tiles with a UTF-8 byte count under each tile; matched/kept/removed characters highlighted; live `length` vs `octet_length` tiles. "Next function" button = viz-next.
Playground: `customers(name, email, phone, city)` with messy data; presets: concat & NULL, length vs bytes, clean-up (trim/initcap/lower), split & position, regex phone/email, case-insensitive (lower + citext).
Production: dedupe sign-ups whose emails differ only by case/spaces → normalise + unique index on `lower(email)`.
Pitfalls: `||` with NULL blanks a whole label; `varchar(n)` counts chars not bytes / octet_length surprises; regexp_matches dropping rows; case-insensitive search via `lower()` with no expression index.
Going deeper: Internals *Designing indexes* (expression indexes).

title: 2. numbers-and-math — Numbers and arithmetic
text:
Facts
1. integer/integer truncates toward zero: `7/2` → 3, `-7/2` → -3 (functions-math).
2. `%`/`mod` takes the dividend's sign: `-7 % 3` → -1 (functions-math).
3. Any numeric operand promotes: `7.0/2` → `3.5000000000000000` (numeric); `7/2::float8` → 3.5 (functions-math, typeconv).
4. Literal types: `1` integer, `3000000000` bigint, `1.5` and `1e3` numeric (typeconv, verified pg_typeof).
5. Overflow is an error, never wraparound: `2147483647 + 1` → `integer out of range` (datatype-numeric).
6. float8 is binary: `0.1+0.2` → `0.30000000000000004`; numeric → `0.3`; 10×0.1 summed → `0.9999999999999999` vs `1.0` (datatype-numeric).
7. `numeric(p,s)`: rounds to s decimals, then errors if integer digits > p−s: `12.345::numeric(5,2)` → 12.35, `1234.5::numeric(5,2)` → `numeric field overflow` (datatype-numeric).
8. `round(2.5)` numeric → 3 (ties away from zero); `round(2.5::float8)` → 2 (ties to even) (datatype-numeric).
9. `round(x, -2)` rounds to hundreds; `trunc` cuts; `ceil(-2.3)` → -2, `floor(-2.3)` → -3 (functions-math).
10. `^` is left-associative: `2^3^2` → 64 (functions-math).
11. Division by zero errors for int, numeric and float8 (verified).
12. `random()` is in [0,1); `random(1,6)` is inclusive (PG17+); `setseed` makes it repeatable; not cryptographic (functions-math).
13. `avg(int)` returns numeric; `sum(x)/count(x)` on ints truncates (functions-aggregate, verified 1 vs 1.6666666666666667).
14. `money` is locale-dependent; prefer numeric for money (datatype-money).
Visualizer: three tabs. Division lanes (pick a, b: int vs numeric vs float8 result + result type, captured). 0.1 drift slider (float8 vs numeric sum, captured for n=1..10). numeric(p,s) box (steppers for p, s; value picker; exact decimal rounding computed in JS with half-away-from-zero; overflow card). viz-next advances the active control.
Playground: `line_items(price numeric(10,2), qty int, weight_kg real)`; presets: integer division trap, types of literals, float vs numeric, rounding family, numeric(p,s) overflow, percentages without truncation, random.
Production: invoice totals drifting by a cent → numeric(12,2) and round once per line.
Pitfalls: `count_a / count_b` = 0; float money; ratio * 100 order; overflow of int sums/ids.
Going deeper: Internals *Primitive types, alignment and padding*.

section: 3. dates-and-times — Dates, times and time zones
title: 3. dates-and-times — Dates, times and time zones
text:
Facts
1. `timestamptz` stores an instant (UTC internally) and displays it in the session `TimeZone`; the original zone is not kept (datatype-datetime).
2. `timestamp` is wall-clock only; `TIMESTAMP '… +02'` silently drops the offset (datatype-datetime).
3. `timestamp AT TIME ZONE z` → timestamptz; `timestamptz AT TIME ZONE z` → timestamp (functions-datetime).
4. POSIX sign: `AT TIME ZONE '+05'` means UTC−5 (verified 12:00 UTC → 07:00) (datatype-datetime).
5. DST gap: `2026-03-08 02:30` in America/New_York reads as `03:30-04`; overlap `2026-11-01 01:30` reads as `-05` (verified).
6. `+ interval '1 day'` keeps local time; `+ '24 hours'` adds elapsed time: 12:00 vs 13:00 across the gap (functions-datetime).
7. Month arithmetic clamps: Jan 31 + 1 month → Feb 28 (2026), Feb 29 (2024) (functions-datetime).
8. `date - date` → integer days; `date + 30` → date; `date + interval` → timestamp (functions-datetime).
9. `now()` is fixed for the whole transaction; `clock_timestamp()` moves (functions-datetime).
10. `date_trunc('week', …)` → Monday; `date_trunc('day', tstz, 'Asia/Tokyo')` truncates in that zone (functions-datetime).
11. `extract` returns numeric; `dow` Sunday=0, `isodow` Monday=1; `week` pairs with `isoyear` (2027-01-01 is week 53 of 2026) (functions-datetime).
12. `date_bin('15 minutes', ts, origin)` buckets arbitrary strides (functions-datetime).
13. `age('2026-03-01','2026-01-31')` → `1 mon 1 day` (functions-datetime).
14. Use half-open ranges `ts >= start AND ts < end` for days and months (functions-datetime OVERLAPS, rangetypes).
Visualizer: Stepper "one instant, many clocks": lanes UTC / New York / London / Kolkata / Tokyo over a 48 h window; an animated instant marker; ghost markers for a timestamp without zone; AT TIME ZONE type flip badge; DST gap and overlap shading; 1 day vs 24 hours. Extra control: session TimeZone picker that changes the "psql shows" line.
Playground: `events(id, happened_at timestamptz, kind)` with generate_series data; presets: TimeZone display, timestamp vs timestamptz, AT TIME ZONE, DST arithmetic, truncation/extract/date_bin, half-open daily report, now vs clock_timestamp.
Production: daily revenue report off by a day for a non-UTC office → group by `date_trunc('day', ts, 'zone')` and half-open bounds.
Pitfalls: `timestamp` column for events; `BETWEEN '…' AND '…-31'` missing the last day; `'now'` frozen in DEFAULT; DST + '24 hours' in schedules.
Going deeper: Internals *Declarative partitioning and pruning* (half-open range bounds).

title: 4. conditional-logic — Conditional logic
text:
Facts
1. Searched CASE: first true WHEN wins; NULL is not true; no ELSE → NULL (functions-conditional).
2. Simple CASE uses `=`, so `CASE NULL WHEN NULL` does not match (verified `not matched`).
3. All THEN results must share a type: `CASE … THEN 1 ELSE 'a'` errors; `1` vs `2.5` → numeric (typeconv-union-case).
4. `COALESCE` returns the first non-NULL argument, stops evaluating there (functions-conditional).
5. `NULLIF(a,b)` → NULL when equal: `x / NULLIF(y,0)` avoids division by zero (functions-conditional).
6. `GREATEST/LEAST` ignore NULLs (differs from the standard) (functions-conditional).
7. `count(*) FILTER (WHERE …)` conditional aggregates (sql-expressions aggregate FILTER).
8. CASE skips unneeded arms at run time, but a constant `1/0` arm can fail at planning (verified on a table) (functions-conditional, sql-expressions).
9. Boolean expressions can be select-list columns; `(x > 2)::int` → 0/1 (datatype-boolean).
10. `sum` over zero rows → NULL; `coalesce(sum(x), 0)` (functions-aggregate).
11. `IS DISTINCT FROM` treats NULL as a value (functions-comparison).
Visualizer: row walker over 5 orders. Modes: tier CASE, COALESCE chain, safe division with NULLIF, FILTER aggregates. Each step evaluates one row: branches light up true / false / NULL in order, result cell fills in; FILTER mode animates accumulators. viz-next = "Next row".
Playground: `orders(id, customer, status, total, qty, coupon, promo)`; presets mirror the modes plus GREATEST/LEAST, boolean columns, CASE type error.
Production: KPI dashboard query with one pass of FILTER aggregates and NULLIF-protected ratios.
Pitfalls: WHEN order; `CASE x WHEN NULL`; division by zero in ratios; sum of nothing is NULL.
Going deeper: Internals *From SQL text to rows* (constant folding at plan time).

title: 5. casting-and-types — Type conversion
text:
Facts
1. `CAST(x AS t)`, `x::t`, and `t 'literal'` are the same conversion (sql-expressions, typeconv).
2. A quoted literal starts as type `unknown` and takes the type its context needs: `1 = '1'` works (typeconv-overview).
3. No implicit integer → text for functions: `length(12345)` and `substr(1234, 3)` error (typeconv-func).
4. text → integer accepts surrounding spaces, `_` separators and `0x` prefixes, but not `'42.5'` or `'1,234'` (verified).
5. numeric → integer rounds half away from zero (2.5 → 3); float8 → integer rounds half to even (2.5 → 2) (verified).
6. Out of range → error: `'99999'::smallint`, `40000::numeric(4,1)` (datatype-numeric).
7. `varchar(n)`/`char(n)` explicit casts truncate silently: `'abcdef'::varchar(3)` → `abc` (datatype-character).
8. `to_char(1234567.891, 'FM9,999,999.00')` → `1,234,567.89`; too few digits → `###` (functions-formatting).
9. `to_number('$1,234.56','L9,999.99')` → 1234.56; `to_date('14/11/2026','DD/MM/YYYY')`; invalid dates error (functions-formatting).
10. Ambiguous `03/04/2026` depends on `DateStyle` (MDY → March 4, DMY → April 3) (datatype-datetime).
11. `pg_input_is_valid(text, type)` and `pg_input_error_info` test input without raising (functions-info).
12. Text comparison is not numeric: `'10' < '9'` is true (verified).
13. boolean input accepts `yes/no/on/off/1/0/t/f` (datatype-boolean).
14. `->>` on jsonb returns text; cast it before arithmetic (functions-json).
Visualizer: cast matrix, captured with `pg_input_error_info`. Mode A: 12 text inputs × 6 target types (ok / changed / error). Mode B: numeric values from a `numeric` or `double precision` source to integer, smallint, numeric(4,1), real (rounding differences). Click a cell for SQL, result, error text and SQLSTATE. viz-next = "Next cell".
Playground: `staging_orders(raw_qty text, raw_price text, raw_date text, raw_paid text)` from a CSV-like import; presets: cast basics, unknown literals, what fails, validate before casting, to_char/to_number/to_date, DateStyle, JSON at a glance.
Production: importing a messy CSV into typed tables: validate rows with pg_input_is_valid, quarantine the rest.
Pitfalls: one bad row aborts the whole INSERT…SELECT; text sort of numbers; float→int rounding; DateStyle ambiguity.
Going deeper: Internals *JSON vs JSONB*.

title: 6. working-with-json — Working with JSON
text:
Scope split: storage, operators, jsonb_set NULL trap, lax/strict and JSON_TABLE live in Internals *JSON vs JSONB*; GIN internals in *GIN*. This lesson covers building, SQL/JSON functions, shredding, updating, validation and an index decision guide.
Facts (all verified on PG 18.6)
1. `to_jsonb(row)` keys by column name; `row_to_json` returns json and keeps column order (functions-json).
2. `jsonb_agg(x ORDER BY …)`; over zero rows an aggregate returns NULL; LEFT JOIN + jsonb_agg gives `[null]`; `jsonb_agg_strict` does not drop `{"id": null}` objects; `COALESCE(jsonb_agg(x) FILTER (WHERE … IS NOT NULL), '[]')` (functions-aggregate).
3. `jsonb_object_agg(k, v)`: NULL key is an error, NULL value kept; `_strict` drops it (functions-aggregate).
4. `JSON_OBJECT`/`JSON_ARRAY`/`JSON_ARRAYAGG` return json unless `RETURNING jsonb`; JSON_OBJECT NULL ON NULL default, JSON_ARRAY ABSENT ON NULL default (functions-json).
5. `JSON_VALUE` returns text (or RETURNING type), NULL ON ERROR and NULL ON EMPTY by default; non-scalar → NULL; string "3" RETURNING numeric → 3 (functions-json).
6. `JSON_QUERY` returns jsonb; several items need WITH [CONDITIONAL] WRAPPER, otherwise NULL; `EMPTY ARRAY ON EMPTY` (functions-json).
7. `JSON_EXISTS … PASSING v AS name`; lax `$.items.sku` unwraps arrays; strict missing key raises inside jsonb_path_query (functions-json).
8. `IS JSON [OBJECT|ARRAY|SCALAR] [WITH UNIQUE KEYS]` on text (functions-json).
9. `jsonb_to_recordset` casts `"3"` → int 3, missing → NULL; `jsonb_array_elements … WITH ORDINALITY` numbers from 1 (functions-json, queries-table-expressions).
10. `||` shallow, `-` key, `#-` path, `jsonb_insert` (insert_after, errors on existing key), `jsonb_set` no-op on missing parent (functions-json).
11. CHECK constraints with `jsonb_typeof`, `?&`, `NOT JSON_EXISTS(… ? (!exists(@.qty) || @.qty.type() != "number" || @.qty < 1))` (ddl-constraints).
12. Index guide, 20k products, 500 pages: `@>` 500 → 53 (GIN path_ops); `?` 500 → 83 (jsonb_ops only); `@@` equality 500 → 4; `->>` = 500 → 3 (B-tree expr); numeric range 500 → 104; jsonpath range: Seq Scan with every index; top-N 503 → 7 (gin-builtin-opclasses, indexes-expressional).
13. Stored generated column: estimate 50 (exact) vs 100 guess for `->>`, 2 for `@>`; VIRTUAL generated columns cannot be indexed (ddl-generated-columns).
Visualizer: three views. Rows → document (5 fold levels with layoutId animation, empty-group toggle plain / FILTER / FILTER+COALESCE); Path explorer (click nodes of inbox doc 1; 8 function results per path captured); Index guide (8 query shapes, plan + buffers before/after, captured).
Playground: customers/orders/order_items, inbox (2 JSON orders), products (20k jsonb). Presets: rows → JSON, empty groups, SQL/JSON functions, shred and load, update toolkit, validate (DO block with notices), index guide + promote.
Production: account-page API, 9 round trips → 1 statement, `[]` instead of fake order. Pitfalls: `[null]`, JSON_VALUE hides bad data, jsonb_set missing parent, one index for every query.

section: 7. ranges-and-special-types — Ranges and other special types
title: 7. ranges-and-special-types — Ranges and other special types
text:
Facts (verified)
1. Bounds `[ ] ( )`, default `[)`; discrete types canonicalize: `[1,10]` → `[1,11)`, `(1,10]` → `[2,11)`; lower > upper is an error (rangetypes).
2. Omitted bound = unbounded (`upper_inf` true, `upper` NULL); `infinity` is a value (`upper_inf` false); `empty` contains nothing, is contained by everything, sorts first (rangetypes, functions-range).
3. Operators `@> <@ && -|- << >> &< &>`, `+ * -`; union/difference that would leave a gap raise "would not be contiguous" (functions-range).
4. Multiranges: input normalizes `{[1,3),[2,6),[8,9)}` → `{[1,6),[8,9)}`; `range_agg`, `unnest`, `range_merge`, multirange `-` (rangetypes, functions-range).
5. `EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)` needs btree_gist for int; error 23P01 with DETAIL key text; PG18 `PRIMARY KEY (room_id, during WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` creates a GiST index and rejects empty ranges (ddl-constraints, sql-createtable, btree-gist).
6. inet keeps host bits, cidr rejects them; host/network/broadcast/netmask/masklen; `>>=` + `ORDER BY masklen DESC` = longest prefix; GiST `inet_ops` serves `<<` (datatype-net-types, functions-net).
7. Text IPs sort wrongly (`'10.1.2.30' < '10.1.2.4'`).
8. point/box/circle/polygon, `<->`, `@>`, `&&`, `~=` (no `=` for point); GiST on point gives KNN index scan (datatype-geometric, functions-geometry).
9. Composite: `(col).field` in SELECT, `col.field` in UPDATE SET; row `=` with NULL is NULL; row comparison left to right (rowtypes).
10. xml: well-formedness check on input, `xpath`, `XMLTABLE`, `xml_is_well_formed`, `xmlserialize … INDENT` all run (datatype-xml, functions-xml).
Visualizer: Two ranges (drag bounds, bracket toggles, int4range vs numrange, + * - and multirange ops; JS range model in `_range.ts` checked against PG on 22,500 random comparisons, 0 mismatches); Bookings (exclusion-constraint simulator with free time from multirange difference); IP networks (cidr containment tree, longest-prefix match; `_net.ts` checked against PG).
Playground: rooms/bookings (EXCLUDE), price_bands (int4range), subnets/access_log (cidr/inet, 20k rows), stores (5k points), plus composite and xml inline. Presets: basics, operators, multiranges/free time, no double bookings, network, geometry/KNN, composite + xml.
Production: race-free room booking with an exclusion constraint. Pitfalls: closed bounds collide, btree_gist missing, non-contiguous union, IPs as text.

# F3 — Designing a Database (plan)

Audience: new to SQL. Define every term once, show results, end each lesson with one "going deeper" pointer.
All numbers below were checked against PostgreSQL 18 (PGlite) with scratch scripts before writing.

title: 1. keys-and-relationships — Keys and relationships
text:
Facts
1. A primary key = UNIQUE + NOT NULL; one per table; creates a unique B-tree index named `<table>_pkey` (ddl-constraints).
2. Natural key = a real-world value (ISO code, email); surrogate key = a generated value with no meaning (ddl-constraints, ddl-identity-columns).
3. `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` uses an implicit sequence; identity is NOT NULL but not unique on its own (ddl-identity-columns).
4. `uuidv7()` (time ordered) and `gen_random_uuid()` (v4) are built in (functions-uuid).
5. `REFERENCES t` defaults to t's primary key; default FK name `<table>_<col>_fkey` (ddl-constraints, tutorial-fk).
6. Referenced columns must be PK/UNIQUE; referencing columns are NOT indexed automatically (ddl-constraints).
7. FK check is skipped when any referencing column is NULL (MATCH SIMPLE) (ddl-constraints).
8. ON DELETE: NO ACTION (default, 23503, deferrable), RESTRICT (23001, not deferrable), CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT (ddl-constraints).
9. Many-to-many = junction table with two FKs and composite PK (ddl-constraints).
10. One-to-one = FK column that is also UNIQUE (or is the PK) (ddl-constraints).
11. Self-reference: `manager_id REFERENCES employees` (ddl-constraints).
Visualizer: mode toggle 1:N / M:N / 1:1 / self; crow's-foot ER SVG + live row cards; click a row to light up linked rows;
ON DELETE lab (pick action, delete author) shows real error text + SQLSTATE or cascading rows.
Playground: authors / books / tags / book_tags / employees. Presets: join 1:N, junction join, ON DELETE RESTRICT via try(),
CASCADE on junction, self-join manager, catalog of FKs.
Production: missing index on FK → slow parent delete. Pitfalls: unindexed FK, CASCADE surprises, nullable FK, natural key that changes.
Deeper: I1 normalization-constraints.

title: 2. constraints-defaults — Constraints and defaults
text:
Facts
1. NOT NULL → 23502; CHECK → 23514; UNIQUE → 23505; FK → 23503; EXCLUDE → 23P01 (errcodes-appendix).
2. Defaults fill missing columns first; the identity value is drawn even if the row is rejected (ddl-default, observed).
3. CHECK passes when the expression is NULL (ddl-constraints).
4. UNIQUE allows many NULLs; `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` forbids a second NULL (ddl-constraints).
5. UNIQUE / PK create a unique B-tree index (ddl-constraints).
6. PG18 stores NOT NULL in pg_constraint (contype 'n') with names like `accounts_email_not_null` (catalog-pg-constraint).
7. Name constraints with `CONSTRAINT name` so errors are readable (ddl-constraints).
8. Enum invalid input → 22P02; enum values are added with ALTER TYPE ADD VALUE (datatype-enum).
9. Domain = type + constraints, `VALUE` keyword, error 23514 (sql-createdomain).
10. EXCLUDE USING gist (during WITH &&) forbids overlaps (ddl-constraints).
11. Default is evaluated at insert time; `DEFAULT now()` (ddl-default).
Visualizer: gatekeeper. Pick or build a row; it passes defaults → NOT NULL → CHECK → UNIQUE → FK; rejected at the first failing gate
with real message + SQLSTATE; identity counter burns a value each attempt.
Playground: plans + accounts + bookings; presets via try().

title: 3. indexes-101 — Indexes for beginners
text:
Facts (100k customers, 935 heap pages, captured)
- Seq Scan email: cost 0..2185, 935 buffers, Rows Removed 99999.
- Index on email: 3 levels (bt level 2), Index Scan cost 0.42..8.44, 4 buffers.
- signup_date ranges: 1 day 55 rows Bitmap (cost 182.75, 56 heap blocks); 1 year Bitmap 1519; all 5 years → Seq Scan 2435.
- lower(email) cannot use email index → Seq Scan.
- Composite (country, city) serves country+city; leading column matters.
- Index sizes: pk 2.2 MB, email 4.0 MB, table 7.5 MB; inserts slower with each index.
- CREATE INDEX blocks writes, not reads (sql-createindex).
Visualizer: Stepper story over a 935-cell page grid + mini B-tree; stats tiles.

title: 4. views-and-sequences — Views, sequences and identity
text:
Facts: view = stored query, runs each time (sql-createview); auto-updatable rules; CHECK OPTION → 44000; aggregate view
update → 55000; materialized view stores result, REFRESH; sequences never roll back (sql-createsequence); serial =
int + sequence + DEFAULT nextval; identity ALWAYS rejects manual ids (428C9), OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE; serial manual id →
later 23505; RETURNING id; currval session-local; RESTART WITH.
Visualizer: tab 1 sequence lab (insert / rollback / failed insert / manual id, serial vs identity); tab 2 view lens
(base rows, view filter, update through view, insert with/without CHECK OPTION, matview stale/refresh).

title: 5. schema-changes — Changing a schema safely
text:
Facts (100k-row orders, captured with pg_locks + relfilenode)
| op | lock | rewrite |
| ADD COLUMN / const default / NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 | AccessExclusive | no |
| ADD COLUMN volatile default / identity / stored generated | AccessExclusive | yes |
| ALTER TYPE int→bigint | AccessExclusive | yes; varchar(50)→(100), varchar→text: no |
| SET NOT NULL / ADD CHECK | AccessExclusive + full scan |
| ADD CHECK NOT VALID / NOT NULL NOT VALID (PG18) | AccessExclusive, instant |
| VALIDATE CONSTRAINT | ShareUpdateExclusive |
| ADD FK | ShareRowExclusive on both tables; NOT VALID skips scan |
| CREATE INDEX | Share (blocks writes); CONCURRENTLY: ShareUpdateExclusive, not in txn (25001) |
Lock queue: waiting AccessExclusive blocks every later query; `lock_timeout` caps the wait (runtime-config-client).
Visualizer: tab 1 planner (pick op → lock, blocks reads/writes, rewrite, scan, safe recipe); tab 2 lock-queue timeline Stepper.

# F5 (`f4`): Practical SQL Patterns — build plan

Audience: practitioners who already write SQL. Every lesson is one pattern: problem → naive solution and why it breaks →
right solution → measured effect (EXPLAIN buffers / row counts captured from PostgreSQL 18). Depth lives elsewhere; each
lesson ends with a "going deeper" pointer to the Internals lesson: m3/* (joins, windows, recursive CTEs, GROUPING SETS),
m4/index-design, m4/explain-analyze, m5/row-locks-skip-locked, m6/full-text-search.

Shared helpers: `app/src/lessons/f4/_ui.tsx` (ResultTable, Sql, Stat, Btn, PlanBox). All numbers in visualizers come from
the capture scripts run against PGlite (PostgreSQL 18.6) with the same schema as the playground.

---

title: 1. pagination — Pagination: OFFSET vs keyset
text:
Facts
1. Rows skipped by OFFSET still have to be computed inside the server, so a large OFFSET is inefficient (queries-limit.html).
2. LIMIT without a unique ORDER BY returns an unpredictable subset; different LIMIT/OFFSET values can produce different plans and orders (queries-limit.html, sql-select.html).
3. `OFFSET start` rows are skipped before LIMIT counting; `LIMIT ALL`/`NULL` = no limit (queries-limit.html).
4. Row-constructor `<`, `>` compare left to right and stop at the first unequal pair: `(a,b) > (x,y)` is lexicographic (functions-comparisons.html).
5. A row comparison against a multicolumn B-tree index whose column order matches is an index condition (indexes-multicolumn.html, functions-comparisons.html).
6. `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` is the standard spelling; `WITH TIES` needs ORDER BY (sql-select.html).
7. Cursors (`DECLARE … CURSOR`) live only inside a transaction unless `WITH HOLD`, which materializes the rows at commit (sql-declare.html).
8. `count(*)` costs effort proportional to table size; `pg_class.reltuples` is an estimate maintained by VACUUM/ANALYZE (functions-aggregate.html, planner-stats.html).
9. Nulls sort last for ASC; keyset columns should be NOT NULL or handled explicitly (queries-order.html).
10. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports `Buffers: shared hit=` per node; in 18 ANALYZE implies BUFFERS (using-explain.html).
Visualizer: an index strip of 100 000 entries (bucketed). Slider = page number. OFFSET mode lights every entry read and
discarded, keyset mode seeks to the last seen key and reads 10. Tiles: rows read, shared buffers, time (captured for pages
1/10/100/1 000/5 000). Second toggle "insert while paging": a new row lands on page 1 and OFFSET shows a duplicate while keyset does not.
Playground: `events` 100 k rows, index `(created_at, id)`. Presets: OFFSET page 1 vs deep page; keyset; row comparison vs
the broken `a > x AND b > y`; backward page; total count vs estimate; cursor.
Production: activity feed API timing out on deep pages. Pitfalls: non-unique sort key, wrong comparison expansion, mixed
ASC/DESC directions, exact counts on every request.

title: 2. upsert-dedup — Upserts and de-duplication
text:
Facts: ON CONFLICT semantics (arbiter inference, `excluded`, DO UPDATE requires target, WHERE still locks, cardinality
violation, atomic insert-or-update under concurrency) (sql-insert.html). `RETURNING old/new` in 18 (sql-insert.html,
dml-returning.html). MERGE: first matching WHEN clause, cardinality violation, not interchangeable with ON CONFLICT under
concurrency (sql-merge.html). `ctid` changes on UPDATE / VACUUM FULL: use only within one statement (ddl-system-columns.html).
`UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (sql-createtable.html, indexes-unique.html). Expression unique index for case-insensitive
uniqueness (indexes-expressional.html). Sequences consumed by conflicting inserts are not returned (sql-insert/functions-sequence).
Visualizer: two modes. *Upsert*: a batch of incoming rows probes the unique index; each row becomes INSERT, UPDATE, or
skipped (DO UPDATE … WHERE); a duplicate key inside the batch triggers the cardinality error. *Dedup*: rows grouped by
normalized email, `row_number()` labels each, rn > 1 marked for delete, then a unique index locks the door.
Playground: `contacts` with seeded duplicates, `staging` batch. Production: nightly CRM import creating duplicates.

title: 3. pivot-reporting — Pivots and reports
text:
Facts: `FILTER (WHERE …)` per aggregate (sql-expressions.html); crosstab source must be ordered, one-arg form fills left
to right and ignores category; two-arg form maps categories (tablefunc.html); GROUPING SETS / ROLLUP and `grouping()`
(queries-table-expressions.html, functions-aggregate.html); `sum` of no rows is NULL (functions-aggregate.html);
`generate_series` over timestamps (functions-srf.html); `lag` (functions-window.html); window aggregate with empty OVER
for percent of total (tutorial-window.html); `date_trunc` (functions-datetime.html).
Visualizer: long rows (month × channel) fold into a pivot grid; toggles: "date spine" (missing month appears as 0 rather
than vanishing), "ROLLUP totals", "% of total", "vs previous month". Clicking a cell highlights its source rows.
Playground: `orders` 3 000 rows over 2026 with a deliberately empty month for one channel.

title: 4. gaps-and-islands — Gaps and islands
text:
Facts: `row_number()` numbering within a partition (functions-window.html); date − integer = date (functions-datetime.html);
`lag()` default NULL (functions-window.html); running sum = aggregate with ORDER BY and default frame (functions-window.html);
`generate_series` with EXCEPT for missing values (functions-srf.html, queries-union.html); range types, `&&`, `-|-`,
`range_agg` → multirange (rangetypes.html, functions-range.html, functions-aggregate.html); exclusion constraint
`EXCLUDE USING gist (… WITH &&)` (rangetypes.html).
Visualizer: stepper over a user's activity days: sort → row_number → date − rn → group → island lengths. Mode 2:
sessionization with a timeout slider (lag gap > N minutes → new session; running sum = session id).
Playground: `logins(user_id, day)`, `clicks(user_id, ts)`, `bookings(room, during tstzrange)`.

title: 5. hierarchies — Trees and graphs
text:
Facts: recursive CTE evaluation with working table; SEARCH DEPTH/BREADTH FIRST; CYCLE clause (queries-with.html); ltree
labels, `<@`/`@>`, lquery `~`, GiST `gist_ltree_ops`, `nlevel`, `subpath` (ltree.html); B-tree index on parent column
for adjacency lists (indexes-intro.html).
Visualizer: one org tree, three storage models. Click a node to fetch its subtree; adjacency shows recursive iterations
(one index probe per level), ltree shows one range on the path index, closure shows one index lookup on `ancestor`. Move a
subtree: counts of rows each model must rewrite.
Playground: `staff` adjacency (≈ 1 365 nodes, 5 levels), `staff_path` ltree, `staff_closure`.

title: 6. search-patterns — Searching text
text:
Facts: LIKE matches whole string; `_`/`%` (functions-matching.html); `text_pattern_ops` for LIKE in non-C locale
(indexes-opclass.html); pg_trgm extraction rules, `similarity`, `%` threshold 0.3, `<->` KNN with GiST not GIN,
`gin_trgm_ops` for LIKE/ILIKE/regex unanchored, patterns with no trigrams → full index scan (pgtrgm.html); full-text
`to_tsvector @@ websearch_to_tsquery`, `ts_rank` (textsearch-controls.html).
Visualizer: type a query; see its padded trigrams, matching candidates with live similarity (same algorithm as pg_trgm),
and a matrix of which index serves which predicate (captured from EXPLAIN).
Playground: `products` 20 k names (en_US collation column) with pg_trgm.

section: 7. queues-and-locking — Job queues and concurrency patterns
title: 7. queues-and-locking — Job queues and concurrency patterns
text:
Facts: SKIP LOCKED semantics and caveat (sql-select.html); row lock taken by FOR UPDATE held to end of transaction
(explicit-locking.html); advisory locks session vs xact, try variants (functions-admin.html, explicit-locking.html);
LISTEN/NOTIFY delivered on commit, between transactions, payload < 8000 bytes (sql-notify.html); optimistic concurrency
via `UPDATE … WHERE version = $v` (row count 0 → retry) (dml-update.html, mvcc); unique index for idempotency keys and
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (sql-insert.html); partial index on pending rows (indexes-partial.html).
Visualizer (simulated sessions): three modes on a scripted timeline. Lease queue: claim with SKIP LOCKED, commit lease,
a worker crashes, lease expires, job reclaimed, idempotency key blocks the double charge. Optimistic update: two
sessions read version 7, one wins, one gets 0 rows and retries. Singleton job: `pg_try_advisory_lock`.
Playground: `jobs`, `payments(idempotency_key unique)`, `accounts(version)`.

title: 8. performance-checklist — A query performance checklist
text:
Facts: plan anatomy, estimated vs actual rows, `Rows Removed by Filter`, loops multiply (using-explain.html); expression
indexes (indexes-expressional.html); implicit cast prevents index use (typeconv, indexes-types); partial index implication
(indexes-partial.html); pg_stat_statements columns (pgstatstatements.html); `work_mem` and `Sort Method: external merge`
(runtime-config-resource.html, using-explain.html); ANALYZE keeps stats current (planner-stats.html).
Visualizer: EXPLAIN smell detector. Pick one of six captured plans; flagged lines glow with the smell and the rule; toggle
"after fix" for the fixed plan with buffers/time before vs after.
Playground: `users`, `orders` (50 k), pg_stat_statements; presets walk the checklist.

# M1 — Foundations & Process Architecture (build plan)

PGlite facts captured for this module (PostgreSQL 18.6 in WASM, single process):
`pg_stat_activity` shows one row, `backend_type = 'standalone backend'`, pid 42. `shared_buffers` = 16384 × 8 kB (128 MB),
`wal_buffers` = 512 × 8 kB (4 MB, auto = 1/32 of shared_buffers), `transaction_buffers` = 32 (shared_buffers/512),
`io_method = sync`, `max_connections` = 100, `superuser_reserved_connections` = 3. `pg_shmem_allocations`: Buffer Blocks
134,221,824 B, Buffer Descriptors 1,048,576 B (64 B × 16384), XLOG Ctl 4,208,256 B, `transaction` SLRU 529,408 B,
`shared_memory_size` = 145MB. `pg_stat_io` lists 14 backend types including `io worker`, `slotsync worker`, `walsummarizer`.
Default `search_path` in PGlite is `public` (stock initdb: `"$user", public`), so presets set it explicitly.
A 20,000-row table (id, customer_id, md5 note) = 192 pages; first scan after eviction shows `shared read=192`, second `shared hit=192`;
each scan raises `usagecount` by one (2 → 3); CHECKPOINT clears `isdirty`.

---

section: 1. what-is-postgres — What PostgreSQL is: cluster, client/server, a query's round trip
title: 1. what-is-postgres — What PostgreSQL is: cluster, client/server, a query's round trip
text:
Facts
1. A **database cluster** is a collection of databases managed by one server instance; on disk it is one data directory (`PGDATA`). (creating-cluster.html)
2. After initdb a cluster holds `postgres`, `template1`, `template0`. (creating-cluster.html, manage-ag-templatedbs.html)
3. Hierarchy: cluster → database → schema → object. Roles, databases, tablespaces are cluster-wide (`pg_global`). (manage-ag-overview.html)
4. A connection reaches exactly one database; no cross-database queries in one connection. (manage-ag-overview.html)
5. Process per user: the postmaster listens (default port 5432, socket `/tmp/.s.PGSQL.5432`) and forks one backend per connection. (connect-estab.html, tutorial-arch.html)
6. The query text travels as plain text; the client does no parsing. (connect-estab.html)
7. Every message: 1 type byte + Int32 length (includes itself, not the type byte). The StartupMessage has no type byte. (protocol-overview.html)
8. libpq requests protocol 3.0 by default (196608); 3.2 is new in 18 with a variable-length cancel key. (protocol-overview.html)
9. Startup: StartupMessage → auth exchange → AuthenticationOk → ParameterStatus × n → BackendKeyData → ReadyForQuery('I'). (protocol-flow.html)
10. Simple query: Query('Q') → RowDescription('T') → DataRow('D')… → CommandComplete('C') → ReadyForQuery('Z'). Results are text format. (protocol-flow.html)
11. Multiple statements in one Query message run as one implicit transaction. (protocol-flow.html)
12. Backend stages: parse → rewrite → plan → execute. (query-path.html)
13. Each relation is a file `base/<database oid>/<relfilenode>`. (storage-file-layout.html)

Visualizer: Stepper "A query's round trip". Lanes: psql (libpq) | socket | postmaster | backend 4711 | data directory.
Steps 1–11 from TCP connect to Terminate. A wire log lists every message with type byte and length computed from the protocol
rules for the actual strings; clicking a message decodes its bytes. Proves: one fork per connection, text query, exact framing.

Playground: tutorial `weather`/`cities` tables. Presets: who/where am I; databases in the cluster; files on disk
(`pg_relation_filepath`); one statement = one transaction (xid per statement vs BEGIN…COMMIT); `statement_timestamp` vs `clock_timestamp`; protocol-level settings.

Production: connection-string mistakes (wrong database / socket path) → diagnose with `current_database()`, `inet_server_addr()`.
Pitfalls: expecting cross-database joins; DROP DATABASE while connected; trust auth after initdb; one statement vs implicit transaction.

section: 2. process-model — The postmaster and one process per connection
title: 2. process-model — The postmaster and one process per connection
text:
Facts
1. Postmaster = first process; starts auxiliary processes, forks backends on demand. (glossary.html)
2. `max_connections` default 100, postmaster context; sizes shared memory. `superuser_reserved_connections` 3; `reserved_connections` 0 for `pg_use_reserved_connections`. (runtime-config-connection.html)
3. One semaphore per allowed connection/worker, in sets of 16 (+1 magic). (kernel-resources.html)
4. `pg_stat_activity`: one row per server process; `state` active / idle / idle in transaction / idle in transaction (aborted) / fastpath / disabled; `backend_type`. (monitoring-stats.html)
5. `authentication_timeout` 1 min. (runtime-config-connection.html)
6. Shutdown: SIGTERM smart, SIGINT fast, SIGQUIT immediate (children get SIGKILL after 5 s; WAL replay at next start). Never SIGKILL the postmaster. (server-shutdown.html)
7. A crashed backend makes the postmaster terminate all others and reinitialize (`restart_after_crash`, default on). (runtime-config-error-handling.html, kernel-resources.html)
8. OOM killer can kill the postmaster; protect with `oom_score_adj` -1000 + `PG_OOM_ADJUST_FILE`. (kernel-resources.html)
9. `pg_cancel_backend` / `pg_terminate_backend`; cancel uses a separate connection carrying PID + secret key. (functions-admin.html, protocol-flow.html)
10. `postmaster.pid` prevents two instances on one data directory. (server-start.html)
11. Backend memory is private (`pg_backend_memory_contexts`). (view-pg-backend-memory-contexts.html)

Visualizer: live process tree. Buttons: connect client, connect superuser, run query, BEGIN (idle in transaction), disconnect,
kill -9 a backend (crash restart), shutdown smart/fast/immediate. `max_connections` = 6, reserved 1 to show the FATALs.
Live `pg_stat_activity` table under the tree.

Playground: `pg_stat_activity`, `application_name`, backend types from `pg_stat_io`, GUC contexts, memory contexts, wait events.
Production: an API fleet with 40 pods × pool 20 = 800 connections; idle in transaction; fix with pooling and timeouts.
Pitfalls: raising max_connections to 2000; idle in transaction; kill -9; OOM killer.

section: 3. shared-memory — Shared memory: buffers, WAL buffers and the commit log
title: 3. shared-memory — Shared memory: buffers, WAL buffers and the commit log
text:
Facts
1. `shared_buffers` default 128MB, postmaster; start at 25 % of RAM, rarely > 40 %. (runtime-config-resource.html)
2. Each buffer has a descriptor (tag, pin count, usage count, dirty flag); `pg_buffercache` exposes them; usage count 0..5. (pgbuffercache.html)
3. Clock sweep: pinned buffers are skipped, usage count is decremented, the first unpinned buffer at 0 is the victim. Dirty victims must be written (after WAL flush) before reuse.
4. Buffer access strategy rings for large seq scans, VACUUM (`vacuum_buffer_usage_limit` 2MB), COPY, CTAS. (glossary.html)
5. `wal_buffers` -1 → 1/32 of shared_buffers, between 64 kB and one WAL segment (16 MB). (runtime-config-wal.html)
6. SLRU caches: `transaction_buffers` (pg_xact), `subtransaction_buffers`, `multixact_*`, `notify_buffers`, `serializable_buffers`, `commit_timestamp_buffers`; `pg_stat_slru`. (runtime-config-resource.html, monitoring-stats.html)
7. pg_xact keeps 2 bits per transaction: in progress / committed / aborted / sub-committed. (storage-file-layout.html)
8. `pg_shmem_allocations` lists the main segment; DSM is separate. (view-pg-shmem-allocations.html)
9. Local memory: `work_mem` 4MB per sort/hash node, `hash_mem_multiplier` 2.0, `maintenance_work_mem` 64MB, `temp_buffers` 8MB. (runtime-config-resource.html)
10. Huge pages (`huge_pages = try`); `shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages`. (kernel-resources.html)

Visualizer: clock-sweep simulator: 16-buffer ring, clock hand, pins, usage counts, dirty flags; workloads hot set / seq scan
(with ring toggle); bgwriter pass; checkpoint. Stats tiles: hits, misses, evictions, backend writes. Shared memory map with real sizes.
Playground: pg_buffercache on a 192-page table: read → hit → usagecount → dirty → checkpoint → evict.
Production: nightly report scan evicting the hot set; ring buffers / pg_prewarm / sizing.
Pitfalls: shared_buffers 80 % of RAM; work_mem × nodes × connections; hit ratio misread; transparent huge pages.

title: 4. background-processes — The background crew
text:
Facts
1. Auxiliary processes: autovacuum launcher, bgwriter, checkpointer, logger, startup, archiver, walreceiver, walsummarizer, walwriter. (glossary.html)
2. bgwriter: `bgwriter_delay` 200ms, `bgwriter_lru_maxpages` 100, `bgwriter_lru_multiplier` 2.0. (runtime-config-resource.html)
3. checkpointer: `checkpoint_timeout` 5min, `max_wal_size` 1GB, `checkpoint_completion_target` 0.9. (wal-configuration.html)
4. walwriter: `wal_writer_delay` 200ms; async commit loss window up to 3 × delay. (wal-async-commit.html)
5. autovacuum launcher: `autovacuum_naptime` 1min, `autovacuum_max_workers` 3; threshold 50 + 0.2 × reltuples. (routine-vacuuming.html)
6. Cumulative stats live in shared memory, flushed by each process at most once per second; written to `pg_stat` on clean shutdown. (monitoring-stats.html)
7. archiver runs `archive_command` / `archive_library` per completed segment. (continuous-archiving.html)
8. PG18 AIO: `io_method` worker (default) / io_uring / sync; `io_workers` 3; `pg_aios`. (runtime-config-resource.html, view-pg-aios.html)
9. `pg_stat_bgwriter`, `pg_stat_checkpointer`, `pg_stat_io` (backend_type × object × context). (monitoring-stats.html)
10. logical replication launcher starts apply workers for subscriptions. (logical-replication-architecture.html)

Visualizer: Stepper over a process/memory/disk diagram: UPDATE dirties a page and writes WAL → COMMIT flush → walwriter →
bgwriter round → io workers read ahead → stats flush → autovacuum → checkpoint (spread, fsync, checkpoint record) → archiver.
Each step shows the governing GUC.
Playground: settings, pg_stat_io by backend type, pg_stat_bgwriter/checkpointer, autovacuum threshold per table, pg_stat_wal.
Production: checkpoint spikes from `max_wal_size` too small → `num_requested` vs `num_timed`.
Pitfalls: disabling autovacuum; checkpoints too frequent; backends doing their own writes; failing archive_command filling pg_wal.

section: 5. databases-schemas-roles — Databases, schemas, search_path and roles
title: 5. databases-schemas-roles — Databases, schemas, search_path and roles
text:
Facts
1. CREATE DATABASE copies `template1` by default; template0 for new encoding/locale; no other sessions on the source. (manage-ag-templatedbs.html)
2. Database-level GRANTs are not copied. `datallowconn` false on template0. (manage-ag-templatedbs.html)
3. search_path default `"$user", public`; first match wins; first existing schema is the creation target. (ddl-schemas.html)
4. pg_catalog searched implicitly first unless listed; pg_temp first for relations. (ddl-schemas.html, runtime-config-client.html)
5. Schemas you lack USAGE on are silently skipped (`current_schemas`). (verified in PGlite)
6. PG15+: PUBLIC lacks CREATE on public; public owned by `pg_database_owner`. (ddl-schemas.html, predefined-roles.html)
7. Roles are cluster-wide; CREATE USER = CREATE ROLE … LOGIN. (database-roles.html)
8. Membership options INHERIT / SET / ADMIN; LOGIN, SUPERUSER, CREATEDB, CREATEROLE never inherited. (role-membership.html)
9. Predefined roles: pg_read_all_data, pg_monitor, pg_signal_backend, pg_maintain… (predefined-roles.html)
10. pg_hba.conf: first matching line wins, no fall-through, no match = reject. `pg_hba_file_rules`. (auth-pg-hba-conf.html)
11. Default PUBLIC privileges: CONNECT/TEMP on databases, EXECUTE on functions, USAGE on types/languages. (ddl-priv.html)

Visualizer: three modes — search_path resolver (role, path, name; animated walk with skip reasons), pg_hba first-match
(client attempt vs rules), role graph (joe/admin/wheel/island from the docs).
Playground: try() helper returning SQLSTATE; roles, schemas, GRANT USAGE, SET ROLE, current_schemas, pg_hba_file_rules.
Production: multi-tenant schema-per-tenant with `ALTER ROLE … SET search_path`; read-only reporting role via pg_read_all_data.
Pitfalls: CREATE on public in upgraded DBs; search_path hijack in SECURITY DEFINER; hba order; DROP ROLE with owned objects.

section: 6. normalization-constraints — Modelling data: normalization and constraints
title: 6. normalization-constraints — Modelling data: normalization and constraints
text:
Facts
1. CHECK passes on true or NULL. (ddl-constraints.html)
2. NOT NULL; at most one explicit not-null constraint per column; named NOT NULL in 18 (`contype = 'n'`). (ddl-constraints.html)
3. UNIQUE builds a unique B-tree; NULLs distinct unless `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. (ddl-constraints.html)
4. PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL, one per table. (ddl-constraints.html)
5. FK actions NO ACTION (default, deferrable) / RESTRICT / CASCADE / SET NULL / SET DEFAULT; referencing columns not indexed automatically. (ddl-constraints.html)
6. DEFERRABLE only for UNIQUE, PK, EXCLUDE, FK. (sql-createtable.html)
7. EXCLUDE USING gist. Temporal keys `WITHOUT OVERLAPS` (18) → GiST, 23P01. (sql-createtable.html)
8. Generated columns: VIRTUAL default in 18, STORED; immutable functions only. (ddl-generated-columns.html)
9. Identity columns ALWAYS / BY DEFAULT; NOT NULL but not unique automatically. (ddl-identity-columns.html)
10. NOT ENFORCED for CHECK and FK (18). (sql-createtable.html)

Visualizer: normalization stepper: messy order sheet (0NF) → 1NF → anomalies → 2NF → 3NF → constraints. Columns animate
between tables with layoutId; functional dependency colouring.
Playground: the 3NF schema with try() to show each constraint's SQLSTATE; generated virtual column; temporal key.
Production: an e-commerce order table with denormalized customer data drifting; split + FK + backfill.
Pitfalls: unindexed FK; CHECK with NULL; UNIQUE with NULLs; NOT ENFORCED lying to the planner.
