# Module 2 — Storage & Page Layout Internals (plan)

All numbers below were measured on PGlite (PostgreSQL 18.6, wasm32, MAXALIGN 8, 8 KB blocks) unless marked "docs".
Lesson 5 (`slotted-page`) is the finished reference lesson.

section: 1. primitive-types — Primitive types, alignment and padding
title: 1. primitive-types — Primitive types, alignment and padding
text:
Facts
- smallint 2 B, integer 4 B, bigint 8 B; out-of-range raises an error (datatype-numeric).
- numeric: 2 bytes per 4 decimal digits + 3–8 B overhead; exact; slow (datatype-numeric). Measured on disk: `1` → 5 B, `123456789` → 9 B.
- real 4 B / double 8 B IEEE 754; `0.1+0.2 = 0.3` is false for float8, true for numeric (datatype-numeric).
- numeric rounds ties away from zero, float to even: `round(2.5::numeric)`=3, `round(2.5::float8)`=2 (datatype-numeric).
- money 8 B, locale-dependent output via `lc_monetary` (datatype-money).
- text/varchar: 1-byte header up to 126 B, 4-byte header beyond; no speed difference between text/varchar/char(n) (datatype-character).
- boolean 1 B; date 4 B; timestamp/timestamptz 8 B; interval 16 B; uuid 16 B (datatype-*).
- `pg_type.typlen` / `typalign` (c=1, s=2, i=4, d=8) drive layout; each fixed column starts at a multiple of its alignment (storage-page-layout, catalog-pg-type).
- Short (1-byte header) varlenas are not aligned (storage-toast).
- Tuple header 23 B → `t_hoff` 24 (storage-page-layout). Row length is MAXALIGNed on the page, plus a 4-byte line pointer.
- Measured: `(bool, int8, int2, timestamptz, int4, text 'hello', bool)` = 67 B; reordered widest-first = 54 B.
Visualizer: column-order padding calculator. Column chips (add / remove / move), an 8-byte-row byte map with padding cells, "sort by alignment" button, live tuple length, MAXALIGNed size, rows per page. Algorithm mirrors heap_fill_tuple; validated against `pg_column_size(row(...))`.
Playground: `typlen/typalign` catalog query, pg_column_size per type, bad vs good ordering on real tables (lp_len), float vs numeric, money and rounding, overflow.
Production: a metrics table with 200 M rows where reordering removes padding.
Pitfalls: float for money; `char(n)` padding; assuming reordering always helps (MAXALIGN rounding); money and locale.

title: 2. arrays — Arrays
text:
Facts
- Any base/enum/composite/range/domain can be an array element; declared sizes and dimensions are not enforced (arrays).
- Subscripts are 1-based; out-of-range reads return NULL (arrays).
- On-disk ArrayType: varlena header 4, ndim 4, dataoffset 4, elemtype 4, then dims[ndim] and lbound[ndim] (4 B each), an optional null bitmap, data (array.h).
- Measured: `'{1,2,3}'::int4[]` = 36 B in memory, 33 B in a row (1-byte header); `'{1,NULL,3}'` = 40; `'{{1,2},{3,4}}'` = 48; `'{}'` = 16.
- NULL elements take no data space, only a bitmap bit (measured).
- `@>`, `<@`, `&&`, `= ANY`; `array[1,2] || 3`, `array_append(…, NULL)` (functions-array, arrays).
- GIN `array_ops` indexes `@> <@ && =` (gin-builtin-opclasses); `= ANY` is not GIN-indexable.
- "Arrays are not sets"; element searches can mean misdesign (arrays).
- unnest / array_agg / WITH ORDINALITY (functions-array).
Visualizer: two modes. (a) Byte layout of a chosen array value (header fields, dims, lbounds, null bitmap, aligned elements), sizes measured. (b) GIN lookup stepper: rows with tag arrays → key → posting list → intersect for `@>`.
Playground: layout + sizes, operators, unnest/array_agg, GIN with EXPLAIN, normalized alternative.
Production: a tagging feature: GIN on text[] vs join table.
Pitfalls: `= ANY` not using GIN; whole-array rewrite on update; NULL concatenation; 1-based / lbound surprises.

title: 3. json-jsonb — JSON vs JSONB
text:
Facts (datatype-json, functions-json, gin-builtin-opclasses)
- json stores exact text; jsonb stores a decomposed binary tree.
- jsonb drops whitespace, sorts object keys (shorter first, then bytewise), keeps the last duplicate key.
- Measured: `{"user":"ana","plan":"pro","user":"ana2",...}` keeps both users in json, only `ana2` in jsonb.
- jsonb can be larger than json for small documents (measured 75 vs 124 B).
- Operators `-> ->> #> #>> @> ? ?| ?&`; `@>` containment semantics.
- `jsonb_ops` indexes keys and values separately (supports `? ?| ?& @> @? @@`); `jsonb_path_ops` hashes each path→value (only `@> @? @@`), smaller.
- `body->>'plan' = 'pro'` cannot use a GIN on body; rewrite as `@>` or add an expression index.
- jsonpath lax (default) vs strict; JSON_TABLE, JSON_EXISTS, JSON_VALUE, JSON_QUERY.
- Large jsonb is TOASTed and compressed like any varlena; any update rewrites the whole value.
Visualizer: side-by-side normalizer (pick a sample doc; animate key reorder, dedup, whitespace), measured sizes; then GIN key extraction for both opclasses.
Playground: normalization, operators, GIN plans, jsonpath lax/strict, JSON_TABLE.

title: 4. uuid-v4-v7 — UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7
text:
Facts (datatype-uuid, functions-uuid)
- 128-bit, 16 B; text form is 36 chars (40 B as text measured).
- `gen_random_uuid()` = `uuidv4()`; `uuidv7([shift])`; `uuid_extract_version`, `uuid_extract_timestamp` (v1/v7 only).
- v7 layout: 48-bit Unix ms, 4-bit version, 12-bit sub-ms fraction, 2-bit variant, 62 random bits.
- Values from one session are monotonic (measured: rand_a steps 000, 001, 002 within a millisecond).
- Measured 50k rows: index pages bigint 139, v7 194, v4 271; leaf fill v7 89.8%, v4 64.2%.
Visualizer: live bit-field explorer (generate v4/v7 in browser, decode fields + timestamp) plus a leaf-locality mini-sim with heat map.
Playground: generate/extract, ordering, index size and fill comparison, uuidv7(shift).

title: 6. tuple-header — xmin, xmax, ctid, infomask
text:
Facts (storage-page-layout, pageinspect, htup_details.h)
- 23-byte header fields; t_cid overlays t_xvac; t_hoff = 24 without a null bitmap, 24 with ≤ 8 columns + bitmap, 32 with 9–72 columns + bitmap (measured).
- Null bitmap: 1 bit per column, 1 = not null.
- Hint bits XMIN_COMMITTED / XMIN_INVALID / XMAX_COMMITTED / XMAX_INVALID are set by readers.
- FROZEN = XMIN_COMMITTED | XMIN_INVALID.
- Row locks live in xmax with LOCK_ONLY; FOR UPDATE also sets KEYS_UPDATED.
- infomask2 low 11 bits = natts; HOT_UPDATED, HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE, KEYS_UPDATED.
Visualizer: 16-bit infomask/infomask2 grids through 11 captured steps; clickable bits.

title: 7. toast — TOAST
text:
Facts (storage-toast, sql-altertable, sql-createtable, runtime-config-client)
- Threshold 2032 B; target 2032 B (toast_tuple_target). Chunks 1996 B, 4 per TOAST page (lp_len 2032).
- 18-byte on-disk pointer: toast relid, value id, raw size, ext size, compression.
- PLAIN / MAIN / EXTERNAL / EXTENDED. pglz default; lz4 needs build support (not in PGlite).
- Measured: 9000 B repetitive text → 122 B inline pglz; 9600 B md5 text → 5 chunks, 18 B pointer.
- toast_tuple_target 4000 keeps a 3040-byte row inline; 256 pushes both columns out of a 2.5 kB row.
- Unchanged TOAST value is reused on UPDATE (same chunk_id).
- Max value 1 GB.

title: 8. fsm-vm-forks — Files, forks, FSM, VM
text:
Facts (storage-file-layout, storage-fsm, storage-vm, storage-init, pgfreespacemap, pgvisibility)
- base/<dboid>/<relfilenode>; forks _fsm, _vm, _init; 1 GB segments; TRUNCATE changes the relfilenode (measured 16442 → 16447).
- FSM: one byte per page (32-byte steps), max-tree inside each FSM page; 3-level FSM (24 KB fork measured).
- VM: 2 bits per heap page; set by VACUUM, cleared by any change.
- DELETE clears VM bits immediately; FSM stays stale until VACUUM (measured).
- Unlogged heap init fork is 0 B, btree init fork is 8 KB.
Visualizer: Stepper over captured runs: files panel, page grid (FSM + VM), FSM max-tree with real node values.

# m3 — Querying & Data Manipulation (build plan)

All numbers below were captured on PGlite (PostgreSQL 18) with the scripts in the scratchpad (`m3/*.sql`).

section: 1. dml-lifecycle — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE: what really happens
title: 1. dml-lifecycle — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE: what really happens
text:
Facts
1. UPDATE writes a new row version and stamps the old one's `xmax`; DELETE only sets `xmax` (storage-hot, dml-update).
2. `RETURNING` works on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE; unqualified columns are NEW for INSERT/UPDATE, OLD for DELETE (dml-returning).
3. PG18: `old.*` / `new.*` in RETURNING; old is NULL for INSERT, new is NULL for DELETE; `RETURNING WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n)` renames (dml-returning, sql-update).
4. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE: old values are non-NULL for conflicting rows (dml-returning).
5. Arbiter = every unique index whose columns exactly match the conflict target; DO UPDATE requires a target; DO NOTHING does not (sql-insert).
6. `EXCLUDED` is the proposed row; it is usable in SET/WHERE of DO UPDATE only, not in RETURNING (sql-insert; verified error).
7. DO UPDATE may not touch the same row twice in one command: cardinality violation (sql-insert).
8. INSERT … ON CONFLICT computes nextval before detecting the conflict, so sequences gap even without aborts (functions-sequence).
9. nextval is never rolled back; a failed INSERT still burns a value (functions-sequence; verified 5→6).
10. MERGE: each candidate row gets one status (MATCHED / NOT MATCHED [BY TARGET] / NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE); first true WHEN wins (sql-merge).
11. MERGE raises cardinality violation if a target row joins several source rows; UPDATE … FROM silently picks one (sql-merge, sql-update).
12. `merge_action()` only valid in MERGE RETURNING (functions-merge-support).
13. Command tags: `INSERT 0 n`, `UPDATE n` counts matched rows even if unchanged, `MERGE n` (sql-insert, sql-update, sql-merge).
14. Each statement outside BEGIN is its own transaction (one xid per statement) (tutorial-transactions).
15. COPY is the bulk path; `ON_ERROR ignore`, `REJECT_LIMIT` (18) (sql-copy).
Visualizer: Stepper over 8 captured statements on `inventory(id identity, sku PK, qty CHECK >= 0)`: line-pointer list with xmin/xmax per version (live/dead/new/lock-only), a RETURNING panel, a sequence counter with burned ids, command tag. Proves: versions not overwrite; RETURNING old/new; upsert gap; MERGE one xid for three actions.
Playground: inventory + delivery + pageinspect; presets: versions, RETURNING old/new, upsert + gap, MERGE + merge_action, cardinality violation, data-modifying CTE move.
Production: idempotent stock ingestion with upsert from a staging table; MERGE with NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE for sync.
Pitfalls: gaps assumed gapless invoice numbers; upsert batch with duplicate keys; UPDATE … FROM multi-match; mass UPDATE bloat (batch).

title: 2. joins — Joins, visualized
text:
Facts: CROSS = N×M; INNER pairs where ON is true; LEFT adds unmatched left NULL-extended; RIGHT mirrored; FULL both; ON filters before the join, WHERE after (queries-table-expressions); USING merges columns, NATURAL joins on all same-named columns and becomes CROSS JOIN with none; NULL = NULL is not true so NULL keys never match; EXISTS = semi-join, NOT EXISTS = anti-join (functions-subquery); JOIN binds tighter than comma; alias hides table name; self-join needs aliases.
Visualizer: teams (4) × players (5, two NULL team_id). Join-type toggle (INNER/LEFT/RIGHT/FULL/CROSS/SEMI/ANTI) and filter toggle (none / `AND p.active` in ON / `WHERE p.active`). Step through each left row: comparisons drawn as lines, result rows appear, NULL-extended rows highlighted. Counts: inner 3, left 5, right 5, full 7, cross 20, semi 2, anti 2; ON-filter 4 vs WHERE-filter 2.
Playground: teams/players/countries; presets per join, ON vs WHERE, NATURAL trap, self-join manager, anti-join plan.
Production: "customers without orders this month" report that silently dropped rows when filter moved to WHERE.
Pitfalls: WHERE on nullable side; NATURAL JOIN new column; fan-out double counting; NULL keys.

title: 3. subqueries — scalar, IN, EXISTS, ANY/ALL
text:
Facts (functions-subquery, functions-comparisons): EXISTS true iff ≥1 row, never NULL, stops early; IN = `= ANY`; NOT IN = `<> ALL`; NOT IN returns NULL when no match and the list has a NULL; empty subquery: IN false, NOT IN true, ALL true, ANY false; scalar subquery: >1 row is an error, 0 rows gives NULL; correlated subqueries re-run per outer row (SubPlan); planner turns IN/EXISTS into Semi Join and NOT EXISTS into Anti Join, but NOT IN stays a hashed SubPlan filter.
Verified: 4,996-row customers, 3 refunds incl. NULL → NOT IN returns 0 rows, NOT EXISTS 4285.
Visualizer: outer customers 1..4, subquery `refunds.customer_id` = {2, 4, NULL} with NULL toggle; operator toggle (NOT IN / NOT EXISTS / IN / EXISTS); per-row step shows expansion `1 <> 2 AND 1 <> 4 AND 1 <> NULL` → three-valued result → kept/dropped, plus the captured plan shape.
Production: suppression list query returning zero rows after one NULL row landed.

title: 4. ctes — inlined vs MATERIALIZED
text:
Facts (queries-with, sql-select): non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced once is folded; referenced twice it is materialized; MATERIALIZED forces a fence; NOT MATERIALIZED forces folding; volatile functions prevent folding; before v12 always a fence; data-modifying CTEs run once to completion, share one snapshot, see each other only via RETURNING; DML in WITH only at top level; same row modified twice unsupported.
Captured on orders(20,000 rows, index on customer_id): inline → Bitmap Index Scan, 40 rows, shared hit=42; MATERIALIZED → CTE Scan, Seq Scan 20,000 rows, Rows Removed 19,960, 1066kB, hit=128; double reference → CTE Scan ×2; NOT MATERIALIZED → index scan on one side.
Visualizer: Stepper over 5 plan trees (plus the data-modifying CTE snapshot step) with rows-per-node bars.

title: 5. recursive-ctes
text:
Facts (queries-with): non-recursive term UNION [ALL] recursive term; iterative algorithm with working and intermediate tables; UNION discards duplicates of any previous row; stops when the working table is empty; breadth-first output is an implementation detail; SEARCH DEPTH/BREADTH FIRST BY … SET col; CYCLE col SET is_cycle USING path; LIMIT in parent only for testing; only one self-reference; recursive DML not allowed.
Verified: org chart under Raj → 6 rows, depth 0..3; routes A→B→C→A, C→D: UNION (node only) → A,B,C,D; UNION ALL + hops → infinite; CYCLE → 5 rows, A at hop 3 marked.
Visualizer: mode toggle tree / graph-UNION ALL / graph-UNION / graph-CYCLE; steps = iterations showing working table, intermediate table, result, highlighted nodes.

title: 6. window-functions
text:
Facts (functions-window, sql-select, sql-expressions): window functions run after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING; do not collapse rows; peers = equal ORDER BY values; default frame RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW (last peer); without ORDER BY whole partition; ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS; RANGE offset needs exactly one ORDER BY column (verified error); EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW/GROUP/TIES; first/last/nth_value see the frame; rank functions agree for peers; WINDOW clause.
Verified on 11 products: running sum with default frame 3550 for all three 700 rows; Laptop last_value default = Sony VAIO for both peers.
Visualizer: frame explorer: click a row, choose mode, start/end bounds and offsets, exclusion, optional partition; frame and peers highlighted; live sum/count/first/last/nth values and rank columns.

title: 7. lateral
text:
Facts (queries-table-expressions, sql-select): LATERAL subquery can reference earlier FROM items; per-row evaluation; functions in FROM are implicitly lateral; LEFT JOIN LATERAL … ON true keeps rows with empty results; WITH ORDINALITY adds bigint ordinality; RIGHT JOIN LATERAL cannot reference left; plan = Nested Loop.
Verified: without LATERAL → "invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table a"; CROSS JOIN LATERAL top-2 → 5 rows, LEFT JOIN LATERAL → 6 rows with Umbrella NULL.
Visualizer: outer row loop; for each account run the subquery with `a.id` bound, show its result, append to output; toggle CROSS vs LEFT and limit 1/2/3.

title: 8. aggregates-grouping
text:
Facts (functions-aggregate, queries-table-expressions): aggregates except count return NULL on empty input; count(*) counts rows, count(col) non-null; FILTER; ordered-set aggregates (percentile_cont interpolates, percentile_disc picks, mode); GROUPING SETS ≡ UNION ALL of groupings; ROLLUP = prefixes, CUBE = power set; grouping() bitmask rightmost = LSB; HAVING filters groups; aggregates cannot be in WHERE; DISTINCT ON keeps first row per key in ORDER BY order.
Verified: items_sold with ('Baz', NULL, 8) → CUBE has two `(NULL, NULL)` rows: 8 (g=2) and 58 (g=3).
Visualizer: grouping-set builder: ROLLUP / CUBE / custom sets toggles, lattice of sets, step through each set showing which input rows fold into which output rows, grouping() bits.

# Module 4 — Query Planner, Optimizer & Indexing Internals (plan)

All numbers below were captured on PGlite (PostgreSQL 18.6) while planning. Lesson files: `app/src/lessons/m4/<slug>.tsx`.
`btree` is DONE (reference lesson) and is not touched.

section: 1 query-pipeline — From SQL text to rows
title: 1 query-pipeline — From SQL text to rows
text:
Facts (docs: query-path, parser-stage, rule-system, planner-optimizer, executor, sql-prepare, runtime-config-query, geqo)
1. Five stages: connection → parser → rewriter → planner/optimizer → executor (query-path).
2. Raw parsing (`scan.l` lexer + `gram.y` bison grammar) uses only syntax rules and makes **no catalog lookups** (parser-stage).
3. Reason: catalog lookups need a transaction; raw parsing alone is enough to recognise BEGIN/ROLLBACK (parser-stage).
4. Parse analysis turns the raw tree into a **query tree**: resolves tables, columns, types; `FuncCall` → `FuncExpr` or `Aggref` (parser-stage).
5. The rewriter's input and output are both query trees; a view is a `_RETURN` rule expanded like a macro (rule-system).
6. The planner first builds cheap **paths**, one per way to scan each relation; a seq scan path always exists (planner-optimizer).
7. Join search is near-exhaustive dynamic programming below `geqo_threshold` (12 FROM items); GEQO above (runtime-config-query, geqo).
8. Three join methods: nested loop, merge join, hash join (planner-optimizer).
9. Executor is a **demand-pull** pipeline: each call returns one more row or NULL (executor).
10. PREPARE does parse+analyze+rewrite once; EXECUTE plans and runs (sql-prepare).
11. `plan_cache_mode = auto`: first 5 executions custom, then generic if its cost is not much higher than the custom average (sql-prepare).
Visualizer: Stepper conveyor over one real query (view `big_orders` joined to `customers`): text → tokens → raw parse tree → query tree (OIDs, types) → rewritten (view inlined) → paths with real costs (hash 2022.47, merge 2787.77, nested loop 3528.49) → plan tree → executor pull (rows climbing the tree). Second mode: plan cache timeline (by_cust switches to generic at execution 6; by_status stays custom).
Playground: customers/orders/view. Presets: raw vs analyzed errors (syntax vs unknown column), view rewrite in EXPLAIN VERBOSE, join methods via enable_*, PREPARE + pg_prepared_statements counts, EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN).
Production: ORM prepared statement with skewed status flips to a bad generic plan → `plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` for that role.
Pitfalls: generic plan on skewed data; >12-table joins hit GEQO; views are not materialized; parse errors vs analysis errors.

title: 2 cost-model — The cost model
text:
Facts (runtime-config-query, using-explain, index-cost-estimation, sql-explain)
1. Costs are arbitrary units; `seq_page_cost = 1.0` is the unit. 2. Defaults: random_page_cost 4.0, cpu_tuple_cost 0.01, cpu_index_tuple_cost 0.005, cpu_operator_cost 0.0025, effective_cache_size 4GB.
3. Seq scan = pages × seq_page_cost + rows × cpu_tuple_cost (+ rows × cpu_operator_cost per qual). Real: 935 + 1000 = 1935; with filter 2185.
4. Startup vs total cost; LIMIT interpolates; EXISTS uses startup cost.
5. Index scan heap cost interpolates between correlated (sequential) and uncorrelated (random) by correlation².
6. `enable_*` flags only add a disable penalty; plans still form (`Disabled: true`).
7. effective_cache_size allocates nothing. 8. random_page_cost per tablespace. 9. Lower random_page_cost → index scans win more often.
Visualizer: real PGlite cost grid (2 tables × 10 random_page_cost values × 3 plan types × 19 selectivities). Sliders for selectivity and random_page_cost, toggle correlated vs scattered column; curves of seq/index/bitmap cost with crossover; live seq-scan formula.
Pitfalls: SSD left at 4.0; benchmarking enable_seqscan=off; comparing costs across queries.

title: 3 statistics — Planner statistics
text:
Facts (planner-stats, planner-stats-details, row-estimation-examples, view-pg-stats, sql-analyze, multivariate-statistics-examples, sql-createstatistics)
1. ANALYZE samples 300 × max target rows. 2. default_statistics_target 100 = max MCVs and histogram buckets. 3. n_distinct > 0 count, < 0 fraction, −1 unique.
4. `=` on an MCV: selectivity = its frequency. 5. Not an MCV: (1 − Σmcf − null_frac)/(n_distinct − #mcv).
6. `<`: Σ matching MCV freqs + histogram fraction × (1 − Σmcf). Histogram excludes MCVs; linear inside a bucket.
7. AND multiplies (independence). 8. Extended stats: dependencies, ndistinct, mcv; need ANALYZE after CREATE STATISTICS. 9. correlation feeds index cost.
Visualizer: real pg_stats for `trips.zone` (statistics target 10): MCV bars + histogram buckets; mode `=` / `<` / two columns; draggable constant shows formula and PostgreSQL's real estimate vs actual count. Extended-stats mode: 1 vs 100.
Pitfalls: stale stats after bulk load; correlated columns; n_distinct misestimates; expression index needs ANALYZE.

title: 5 hash-index
text:
Facts (hash-index, sql-createindex, pageinspect): 4-byte hash only; lossy; `=` only; no unique/multicolumn; metapage/bucket/overflow/bitmap pages; maxbucket/highmask/lowmask; one bucket split at a time, foreground; never shrinks; empty index starts with 8 buckets (maxbucket 7), ffactor 307 for int4 and split at ntuples > ffactor × (maxbucket+1) (real: 2457 rows → maxbucket 8).
Visualizer: live linear-hash sim with real `hashint4` codes, small pages; insert keys, insert duplicates (overflow chain), split animation.
Pitfalls: duplicates → overflow chains; growth spikes; expecting smaller than btree for small keys (uuid hash 1040 kB vs btree 632 kB at 20k rows).

title: 6 gin
text:
Facts (gin, sql-createindex, runtime-config-client): entry tree of keys; posting list vs posting tree; pending list with fastupdate (default on), gin_pending_list_limit 4MB, flush on VACUUM/autoanalyze/gin_clean_pending_list/limit; every search scans pending list; opclasses array_ops, jsonb_ops, jsonb_path_ops, tsvector_ops, pg_trgm; consistent/triConsistent with recheck; no index-only scans.
Visualizer: live sim: insert documents (tags) into pending list; flush merges into entry tree; posting list → posting tree at threshold; query `@>` intersects posting lists and scans pending list.
Pitfalls: flush spike; jsonb `->>` equality not indexable by GIN; slow bulk loads; pending list making reads slow.

title: 7 gist-spgist
text:
Facts (gist, spgist, indexes-types, ddl-constraints EXCLUDE): GiST balanced tree of predicates with consistent/union/penalty/picksplit/same; KNN via distance lower bounds; exclusion constraints; SP-GiST quad-tree/k-d/radix, unbalanced, non-overlapping partitions.
Visualizer: 2-D points; GiST R-tree with overlapping MBRs vs SP-GiST quad-tree partitions; step-through KNN best-first search with a priority queue of real distances.

# M5 — Concurrency, MVCC & Locking Internals (build plan)

PGlite facts captured for this module (PostgreSQL 18.6, one backend):
- A fresh read-only transaction has vxid `0/7` and `pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned()` = NULL; the first UPDATE assigns xid 755 and
  adds a `transactionid` ExclusiveLock (fastpath = false). Weak relation locks (AccessShare, RowShare, RowExclusive) show `fastpath = true`;
  `LOCK … IN SHARE MODE` and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE show `fastpath = false`.
- SAVEPOINT + write assigns subxid 756 (second `transactionid` lock); `ROLLBACK TO` drops that lock; bob's old version keeps `xmax = 756`
  (aborted, so ignored). The new version had `cmin = 1` (second command).
- Snapshot text in a quiet single session: `755:755:` (xmin = xmax, empty xip). `pg_visible_in_snapshot(own xid)` = false.
  `pg_visible_in_snapshot(755, '755:760:757')` = true, 757 → false (in xip), 760 → false (≥ xmax).
- SERIALIZABLE: `WHERE id = 1` takes SIReadLock on tuple (0,1) + btree page 1; a `sum()` seq scan promotes to a relation SIReadLock.
- `FOR UPDATE` writes the locker xid into `t_xmax` with `HEAP_XMAX_EXCL_LOCK | HEAP_XMAX_LOCK_ONLY`; pg_locks shows only RowShareLock on the
  table. FOR KEY SHARE then FOR SHARE in a savepoint → `xmax = 1` (MultiXact), `pg_get_multixact_members(1)` = (763 keysh), (764 sh).
- ALTER TABLE: ADD COLUMN, ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID, SET NOT NULL → AccessExclusive; SET STATISTICS, SET (fillfactor), VALIDATE CONSTRAINT →
  ShareUpdateExclusive; CREATE INDEX → Share.
- Advisory: session lock taken twice needs two unlocks (third unlock returns false + WARNING); after ROLLBACK the xact lock is gone, the
  session lock (8) stays.
- HOT (items: id pk, sku indexed, qty): UPDATE qty → lp1 `HEAP_HOT_UPDATED`, ctid (0,4), new tuple `HEAP_ONLY_TUPLE`; no index entry.
  UPDATE sku → new tuple (0,6), **both** indexes get a new entry pointing at (0,6) (pkey has key 2 twice). VACUUM: lp1 → REDIRECT to 5,
  lp2 and lp4 → UNUSED, index entries for (0,2) removed. `n_tup_upd 3, n_tup_hot_upd 2`.
- Fillfactor experiment (10,000 rows, 2 indexes, update 20% of rows, 3 rounds): ff100: round 1 0% HOT, pkey 30 → 57 pages; ff90: 57% HOT
  round 1, 84% after 3; ff80 and below: 100% HOT, indexes unchanged. Rows/page: 88 (100), 79 (90), 70 (80), 62 (70), 53 (60), 44 (50).
  Whole-table UPDATE: only ff50 stays 100% HOT (ff70 → 42%, ff90 → 11%).
- Per-row EXCEPTION block for 500 updates consumed 502 xids (500 subxids); one set-based UPDATE consumed 1.
- `deadlock_timeout` 1s, `lock_timeout` 0, `max_prepared_transactions` 0 (PREPARE TRANSACTION unavailable), `log_lock_waits` off.
  `pg_wait_events`: 84 LWLock, 12 Lock, `SpinDelay` under Timeout.

Shared local components: `_timeline.tsx` (SessionTimeline: lanes A/B/C, ticks, statement cards, wait bars, snapshot/xid badges,
TupleVersions, Graph for waits-for / rw-conflicts), `_matrix.tsx` (clickable conflict matrix for table and row lock modes).

# M6 — Advanced Programmability & Extensions (plan)

Numbers marked "PGlite" were captured from PostgreSQL 18.6 in PGlite while planning.
Shared playground helper used by several lessons: `try_sql(text)`, a PL/pgSQL function that EXECUTEs a statement inside an
EXCEPTION block and returns `OK` or the error text, so presets can show an error without failing.

title: 1. views-matviews — Views and materialized views
text:
Facts
1. A view is a relation with no storage (`relkind = 'v'`, `relfilenode = 0`) plus an `ON SELECT DO INSTEAD` rule named `_RETURN` in `pg_rewrite` (rules-views).
2. The rewriter replaces the view's range-table entry with a subquery holding the rule's stored query tree, then recurses into it (rules-views).
3. Expansion happens before planning, so the planner pulls the subquery up and sees one flat join (rules-views). PGlite: view and hand-written subquery give the same plan, `Hash Join cost=8.32..12.86`, index scan on `orders_pkey`.
4. Privileges on base tables are checked as the view owner unless `security_invoker = true` (sql-createview, rules-privileges).
5. Views hide columns reliably but not rows; `security_barrier` stops cheap user functions running before the view's quals (rules-privileges).
6. Auto-updatable: one FROM item, no WITH/DISTINCT/GROUP BY/HAVING/LIMIT/OFFSET/set ops, no aggregates/window/SRF in the select list (sql-createview).
7. `WITH CHECK OPTION` rejects INSERT/UPDATE rows the view could not see; CASCADED is the default (sql-createview).
8. `SELECT *` in a view is expanded at creation; later table columns do not appear (sql-createview).
9. A materialized view stores rows (`relkind = 'm'`); the rule is used only to populate it (rules-materializedviews).
10. REFRESH replaces contents; plain REFRESH blocks readers; CONCURRENTLY needs a populated matview and a unique, non-partial, column-only index (sql-refreshmaterializedview).
11. `WITH NO DATA` leaves the matview unscannable until refreshed (sql-creatematerializedview).
Visualizer: Segmented view/matview. View mode: Stepper over the query tree (parse, find `_RETURN`, substitute subquery RTE, recurse, planner pull-up, final plan with real costs). Matview mode: Stepper over CREATE (stored heap, relfilenode), SELECT (seq scan of stored rows), base table change (stale), REFRESH (new relfilenode, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE), REFRESH CONCURRENTLY (diff by unique key, EXCLUSIVE, same relfilenode).
Playground: products/orders (200/20k rows), view `order_lines`, matview `daily_revenue`. Presets: pg_rewrite row; view EXPLAIN vs subquery; matview + stale data; CONCURRENTLY fails then works with unique index; relfilenode before/after refresh; WITH CHECK OPTION via try_sql; updatability in information_schema.
Production: dashboard aggregate recomputed on every page load → matview + unique index + REFRESH CONCURRENTLY on a schedule.
Pitfalls: CONCURRENTLY without unique index; SELECT * frozen columns; leaky view without security_barrier; dropping a column used by a view.

title: 2. triggers — Triggers
text:
Facts
1. Trigger functions take no args and return `trigger`; not writable in plain SQL (triggers).
2. Matrix: BEFORE/AFTER ROW on tables and foreign tables; INSTEAD OF ROW on views only; TRUNCATE statement-only; default is FOR EACH STATEMENT (sql-createtrigger).
3. Statement triggers fire once even for zero rows (triggers). PGlite: `UPDATE … WHERE false` fires BEFORE and AFTER STATEMENT.
4. Same-event triggers fire alphabetically by name (triggers).
5. BEFORE ROW returning NULL skips the row and later triggers for it; the returned row replaces NEW (triggers).
6. Row AFTER triggers are queued and fire at the end of the statement, before AFTER STATEMENT (triggers).
7. AFTER trigger WHEN is evaluated right after the row change and decides whether an event is queued (sql-createtrigger).
8. Transition tables: `REFERENCING OLD TABLE … NEW TABLE …`, AFTER only, no column list, single event (sql-createtrigger).
9. BEFORE ROW sees rows processed earlier in the same statement; AFTER ROW sees all changes (trigger-datachanges).
10. Constraint triggers are AFTER ROW and can be deferred to commit (sql-createtrigger).
11. Event triggers: `login`, `ddl_command_start`, `ddl_command_end`, `table_rewrite`, `sql_drop` (event-triggers).
12. No cascade depth limit; recursion is the programmer's problem; `pg_trigger_depth()` helps (triggers).
PGlite firing log for `UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 5` over 3 rows (B-2 goes negative): a_before_stmt; b_touch A-1; c_guard A-1 ok; b_touch B-2; c_guard B-2 skipped; b_touch C-3; c_guard C-3 ok; d_audit A-1; d_audit C-3; e_summary old_rows=2 new_rows=2 delta=-10.
Visualizer: timeline with lanes (statement, per-row BEFORE, AFTER queue, transition tables), steps generated from toggles: guard on/off, WHEN on/off, rename b_touch to z_touch (alphabetical order flips).
Playground: inventory + trigger_log + the five triggers. Presets: firing log; zero-row statement; no-op update and WHEN; pg_trigger catalog; INSTEAD OF trigger on a view; recursion guard with pg_trigger_depth.
Production: audit trail per row vs one statement trigger with transition tables.
Pitfalls: AFTER ROW trigger updating same table (recursion); BEFORE trigger returning NULL by accident; heavy work in row triggers on bulk loads; relying on creation order.

title: 3. plpgsql — PL/pgSQL functions and procedures
text:
Facts
1. Body is a block: `[DECLARE] BEGIN … [EXCEPTION …] END` (plpgsql-structure).
2. First call compiles to an instruction tree; each SQL statement is prepared on first execution via SPI and may get a cached generic plan (plpgsql-implementation).
3. Errors in unvisited code paths surface only when reached (plpgsql-implementation).
4. A block with EXCEPTION is a subtransaction; on error, DB changes inside it roll back but local variables keep their values (plpgsql-control-structures). PGlite: top xid 753, failing block used 754 (aborted), second block 755.
5. EXCEPTION blocks are much more expensive to enter and exit (plpgsql-control-structures). PGlite: 200k loop iterations 17.9 ms plain vs 136.6 ms with an EXCEPTION block.
6. `OTHERS` does not catch `QUERY_CANCELED` or `ASSERT_FAILURE` (plpgsql-control-structures).
7. `RETURN NEXT` / `RETURN QUERY` append to the result set; the function returns at the final RETURN (plpgsql-control-structures).
8. EXECUTE runs dynamic SQL, planned each time; use `format('%I', …)`, `%L`, or `USING` to avoid injection (plpgsql-statements).
9. Procedures called with CALL (and DO) may COMMIT/ROLLBACK; not inside a block with EXCEPTION, not under a SELECT (plpgsql-transactions).
10. Volatility: VOLATILE re-evaluated each row and sees fresh snapshot per query; STABLE/IMMUTABLE use the caller's snapshot and never see the calling command's changes (xfunc-volatility).
11. `'now'` literal in a typed context is frozen at first analysis (plpgsql-implementation).
Visualizer: code panel with a moving cursor, transaction stack (top xid / subxact xids), audit rows with xmin and status, local variables; toggle "with EXCEPTION / without". Cost tiles with measured timing.
Playground: accounts/audit + demo() function. Presets: run demo, xmin of rows, cost of EXCEPTION loop, procedure with COMMIT, dynamic SQL with format, volatility catalog.
Pitfalls: EXCEPTION inside hot loops; SQL injection with string concat; variable/column name conflict; IMMUTABLE lies in indexes.

title: 4. rule-system — The rule system
text:
Facts
1. Rewriter sits between parser and planner and turns one query tree into zero or more (rules).
2. Query tree parts: command type, range table, result relation, target list, qual, join tree (querytree).
3. Non-SELECT rules: ALSO (default) or INSTEAD, optional qual, NEW/OLD, multiple actions; they create new trees (rules-update).
4. Qualified ALSO rule → action tree with rule qual AND original qual, plus the original (rules-update).
5. log_shoelace rewrite: merge range table, add rule qual, add original qual, replace NEW with target-list entries, replace OLD with result relation (rules-update). PGlite EXPLAIN shows `Filter: (6 <> sl_avail)`.
6. ON INSERT: original runs first; ON UPDATE/DELETE: original runs after the actions (rules-update).
7. If NEW column is not in the target list it means OLD (UPDATE): `SET sl_color = 'green'` writes no log (rules-update).
8. Multi-row UPDATE logs with one INSERT … SELECT: 4 rows updated, 3 logged (rules-update). PGlite confirms.
9. Rules are applied in alphabetical order; command status comes from the last INSTEAD query of the same type (rules-status).
10. Volatile functions in NEW can run more than once: serial default evaluated twice (rules-update). PGlite: events ids 1,2 vs copy 3,4.
11. Rules cannot enforce FKs or raise errors; triggers usually better (rules-triggers).
Visualizer: Stepper of the five steps with query-tree cards, Segmented scenario: sl_avail=6, sl_color only, multi-row.
Playground: shoelace schema from the docs. Presets: pg_rewrite, EXPLAIN two plans, log results, no-op color update, multi-row, volatile nextval pitfall, DO INSTEAD NOTHING on a view.
Pitfalls: nextval double evaluation; silent INSTEAD NOTHING; WITH not supported; rules vs RETURNING/COPY.

title: 5. fdw — Foreign data wrappers
text:
Facts
1. SQL/MED objects: wrapper (handler + validator) → server → user mapping → foreign table (ddl-foreign-data, postgres-fdw).
2. Handler returns an `FdwRoutine` of C callbacks; scan callbacks required (fdwhandler).
3. Without a validator, options are not checked (fdw-functions).
4. Planning: GetForeignRelSize → GetForeignPaths → GetForeignPlan; executor Begin/Iterate/ReScan/End (fdw-callbacks).
5. postgres_fdw ships WHERE clauses only with built-in (or listed extension) and IMMUTABLE functions/operators (postgres-fdw).
6. Joins ship when both tables are on the same server and user mapping; aggregates, sorts and LIMIT can ship too (postgres-fdw, fdw-planning).
7. Remote transactions use REPEATABLE READ (SERIALIZABLE if local is), no 2PC (postgres-fdw).
8. `fetch_size` default 100, `batch_size` default 1, `fdw_startup_cost` 100, `fdw_tuple_cost` 0.2, `use_remote_estimate` false (postgres-fdw).
9. Remote session runs with `search_path = pg_catalog`, `TimeZone = UTC` (postgres-fdw).
10. `EXPLAIN VERBOSE` shows the Remote SQL (postgres-fdw).
11. file_fdw reads server files via COPY, read-only, options on the table only (file-fdw).
12. `IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA` creates foreign tables from the remote catalog (sql-importforeignschema).
PGlite: no file_fdw/postgres_fdw. Wrapper without handler can be created; querying raises `foreign-data wrapper "…" has no handler`.
Visualizer: interactive pushdown planner (checkbox quals, ORDER BY, LIMIT, aggregate, join), output Remote SQL, local Filter, simulated rows over the wire (illustrative remote table of 1,000,000 rows).
Playground: wrapper/server/user mapping/foreign tables catalog objects; provolatile check; try_sql shows the no-handler error.
Pitfalls: now() not shipped; collation/type mismatch; READ COMMITTED surprise; N+1 fetches with small fetch_size.

title: 6. extensions — Extensions everyone runs
text:
Facts
1. Extension = control file + `name--version.sql` scripts (+ shared library) (extend-extensions).
2. Member objects are tracked in pg_depend with deptype 'e'; DROP EXTENSION removes them; pg_dump emits only CREATE EXTENSION (extend-extensions). PGlite: pg_trgm 1.6 has 47 member objects.
3. Updates follow the shortest chain of `old--new.sql` scripts; `pg_extension_update_paths` (extend-extensions).
4. `trusted = true` lets non-superusers with CREATE on the database install (pg_trgm, pgcrypto trusted; pg_stat_statements, pageinspect not) (extend-extensions, contrib).
5. pg_stat_statements needs shared_preload_libraries and compute_query_id; one row per dbid/userid/queryid/toplevel (pgstatstatements).
6. Trigram: words padded with two leading spaces and one trailing; similarity = shared / union; threshold 0.3 (pgtrgm). PGlite: similarity('postgres','postgis') = 0.416667.
7. gin_trgm_ops / gist_trgm_ops support LIKE/ILIKE/~ with unanchored patterns; KNN `<->` only with GiST (pgtrgm).
8. pgvector: `vector(n)`, operators `<->` L2, `<=>` cosine, `<#>` negative inner product; HNSW (m=16, ef_construction=64 defaults) and IVFFlat; `hnsw.ef_search` default 40; approximate results.
9. pageinspect, pgcrypto (digest, crypt/gen_salt), pg_buffercache, auto_explain (O-contrib).
Visualizer: tabs: pg_trgm (type two strings, live trigram sets, overlap, similarity, threshold) and HNSW (stepper of a greedy layered search over a 2D graph).
Playground: extensions pg_trgm, vector, pg_stat_statements, pgcrypto, pageinspect.
Pitfalls: pg_stat_statements not preloaded; trigram search on patterns shorter than 3 chars; HNSW recall vs filters; extension upgrades without ALTER EXTENSION UPDATE.

title: 7. full-text-search — Full-text search
text:
Facts
1. Parser tokenizes and classifies; dictionaries normalize to lexemes and drop stop words; tsvector = sorted lexemes with positions (textsearch-intro).
2. Stop words are dropped but still consume positions (textsearch-dictionaries).
3. `'…'::tsvector` does not normalize; `to_tsvector` does (textsearch-intro). PGlite: cast match false, function match true.
4. websearch_to_tsquery: quotes → `<->`, `or` → `|`, `-` → `!`, never errors (textsearch-controls).
5. Expression GIN index needs the 2-argument `to_tsvector` (textsearch-tables).
6. Generated stored tsvector column is the modern pattern (textsearch-tables).
7. GIN: one entry per lexeme with a posting list; GiST: lossy signature, recheck (textsearch-indexes).
8. ts_rank / ts_rank_cd, weights A–D default {0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0} (textsearch-controls).
9. ts_headline uses the original document and is slow; output not XSS-safe (textsearch-controls).
10. Limits: lexeme < 2 KB, 256 positions per lexeme, positions ≤ 16383, tsvector < 1 MB (textsearch-limitations).
Visualizer: 6 docs captured from PGlite: pick doc → token → dictionary → lexeme pipeline; pick query → tsquery → GIN entry lookup → posting lists combined → matches + rank.
Playground: docs with generated tsv and GIN index.
Pitfalls: index not used due to config mismatch; casting text to tsvector; ranking cost over many matches; english stemming of names.

title: 8. row-level-security — Row-level security
text:
Facts
1. ENABLE RLS with no policy = default deny; owner bypasses unless FORCE; superusers and BYPASSRLS always bypass (ddl-rowsecurity).
2. Permissive policies OR together; restrictive AND; at least one permissive needed for any access (ddl-rowsecurity, sql-createpolicy).
3. USING filters existing rows silently; WITH CHECK errors on new rows (sql-createpolicy).
4. FOR ALL/UPDATE with no WITH CHECK reuse USING (sql-createpolicy).
5. Policies are applied before user quals except leakproof ones (ddl-rowsecurity). PGlite plan: `Filter: ((status <> 'archived') AND (tenant_id = …) AND (title ~~ 'L%'))`.
6. `row_security = off` makes filtered queries error instead of bypassing (ddl-rowsecurity). PGlite: `query would be affected by row-level security policy`.
7. FK/unique checks bypass RLS → covert channel (ddl-rowsecurity).
8. Views run with owner privileges unless security_invoker (sql-createview).
9. Policy enforcement for INSERT/UPDATE happens after BEFORE triggers (sql-createpolicy).
Visualizer: live policy combiner: rows table, toggle policies (permissive/restrictive), set role and session vars, see combined expression and filtered rows animate; INSERT check panel.
Playground: tickets, role app_user, policies with current_setting.
Pitfalls: testing as superuser/owner; missing setting → error vs NULL; leaking through unique violations; restrictive-only policies deny all.

# m7 — WAL, Replication, Vacuum & High Availability (build plan)

PGlite facts that shape this module (measured, PGlite 0.5.16 = PostgreSQL 18.6):
`wal_level = replica`, `fsync = off`, `data_checksums = on`, `full_page_writes = on` (cannot be changed), `wal_compression` accepts only `pglz`.
No checkpointer/WAL writer/autovacuum processes run (single "standalone backend"), so nothing vacuums or flushes behind the reader's back.
`pg_get_wal_records_info` reads only flushed WAL, so marks are taken with `pg_current_wal_insert_lsn()` and read up to `pg_current_wal_lsn()` after a commit.
Cumulative stats need `SELECT pg_stat_force_next_flush();` as its own statement before reading `pg_stat_user_tables`.
Logical slots fail ("logical decoding requires wal_level >= logical"); publications, physical slots, `pg_logical_emit_message`, `pg_backup_start/stop`, `pg_create_restore_point`, `pg_switch_wal` all work.
VACUUM VERBOSE output arrives as notices that the playground does not display, so presets read results from `pg_class`, `pg_visibility_map`, `pg_freespace`, `pg_stat_user_tables`.

---

title: 1. wal-lsn — Write-ahead logging and LSNs
text:
Facts
1. WAL rule: data-file changes may be written only after the WAL records describing them are flushed (wal-intro.html).
2. Only the WAL must be flushed at commit; it is sequential, and one flush can commit many transactions (group commit) (wal-intro.html, wal-configuration.html).
3. LSN = byte position in the WAL stream, type `pg_lsn`; subtracting two LSNs gives bytes (wal-internals.html, datatype-pg-lsn.html).
4. Segment files are 16 MB, pages 8 kB; names are 24 hex digits: timeline + segment number (wal-internals.html).
5. Each record has a resource manager (Heap, Btree, Transaction, XLOG…) and a CRC-32C (wal-reliability.html, pgwalinspect.html).
6. `wal_level` minimal < replica (default) < logical; changing it needs a restart (runtime-config-wal.html).
7. `synchronous_commit` levels off/local/remote_write/on/remote_apply; with no sync standbys only on/off differ (runtime-config-wal.html).
8. Async commit risks loss of the last transactions, never corruption; window up to 3 × `wal_writer_delay` (200 ms) (wal-async-commit.html).
9. `commit_delay` (0) and `commit_siblings` (5) widen the group-commit window (wal-configuration.html).
10. Rolled-back transactions still write WAL plus an ABORT record (measured).
Visualizer: Stepper over a captured run (INSERT, HOT UPDATE, DELETE, ROLLBACK, async INSERT). LSN tape with records sized by bytes; insert / write / flush pointers; click a record to decode its LSN into segment file name + offset.
Playground: `accounts` (50 rows, fillfactor 90) + `marks(label, lsn)`. Presets: current LSN and file name; one INSERT's records; UPDATE/DELETE/ROLLBACK records; LSN arithmetic; async commit at-risk bytes; WAL stats by rmgr.
Production: event-ingest service using `SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off` for telemetry, kept on for payments.
Pitfalls: `fsync = off` confused with async commit; WAL on a full disk PANICs; misreading LSN differences across `pg_current_wal_lsn` vs insert LSN.

section: 2. checkpoints-fpw — Checkpoints and full page writes
title: 2. checkpoints-fpw — Checkpoints and full page writes
text:
Facts
1. Checkpoint = all dirty pages flushed + checkpoint record; recovery starts at its redo point (wal-configuration.html).
2. Triggers: `checkpoint_timeout` 5 min or `max_wal_size` 1 GB (soft), whichever first; skipped if no WAL (wal-configuration.html).
3. `checkpoint_completion_target` 0.9 spreads writes; `checkpoint_warning` 30 s (runtime-config-wal.html).
4. Torn pages: 8 kB page = 16 × 512 B sectors; FPI on first modification after a checkpoint (wal-reliability.html).
5. With checksums on, even a hint-bit-only change logs an FPI (`FPI_FOR_HINT`) (runtime-config-wal.html wal_log_hints).
6. `wal_compression` compresses FPIs (pglz/lz4/zstd) (runtime-config-wal.html).
7. pg_control stores the latest checkpoint location; recovery reads pg_control → checkpoint record → redo forward (wal-internals.html).
8. Segments before the redo segment are recycled or removed; `min_wal_size` 80 MB (wal-configuration.html).
9. Standbys perform restartpoints at checkpoint records (wal-configuration.html).
Measured: after CHECKPOINT one HOT UPDATE wrote 14,830 B (heap FPI 6,560 + VM FPI 8,192); the next UPDATE on the same page 77 B; another page 6,633 B. pglz: heap image 4,154 B. Full-table update of 54 pages: 637 kB right after a checkpoint vs 326 kB the second time.
Visualizer: Stepper: checkpoint cycle on a timeline + buffer grid + WAL tape; crash and replay; Segmented `wal_compression` off/pglz changes FPI sizes.
Playground: `sensors` 2000 rows; presets: pg_control_checkpoint; FPI after CHECKPOINT; same page again; pglz; full-table update twice; pg_stat_wal.
Production: IoT platform where `checkpoint_timeout` 5 min caused WAL spikes; raise to 15 min + max_wal_size.
Pitfalls: frequent checkpoints (warning), `full_page_writes = off` on non-atomic storage, completion target 1.0.

title: 3. vacuum — VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL
text:
Facts
1. Four reasons to vacuum: space, stats, VM, wraparound (routine-vacuuming.html).
2. Plain VACUUM takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE; FULL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and writes a new file (routine-vacuuming.html, sql-vacuum.html).
3. Phases: initializing, scanning heap, vacuuming indexes, vacuuming heap, cleaning up indexes, truncating heap, performing final cleanup (progress-reporting.html).
4. Index passes repeat when dead TIDs exceed `maintenance_work_mem` / `autovacuum_work_mem` (progress-reporting.html).
5. Pruning (on access) removes HOT-dead tuples within a page without index work (storage-hot.html).
6. Truncation of empty tail pages needs a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; `vacuum_truncate` / `TRUNCATE false` (sql-vacuum.html).
7. VACUUM sets VM bits and updates the FSM (storage-vm.html, storage-fsm.html).
8. VACUUM FULL progress shows in pg_stat_progress_cluster (progress-reporting.html).
9. `INDEX_CLEANUP`, `PARALLEL`, `SKIP_LOCKED`, `BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT` options (sql-vacuum.html).
10. Cannot run inside a transaction block (sql-vacuum.html).
Measured: 106 pages, 2500 HOT updates + 1500 deletes at the tail; VACUUM: 1500 dead item identifiers on 17 pages, index scans 1, "truncated 106 to 90 pages", 106 set all-visible, 16 all-frozen; FULL: new relfilenode, pkey 30 → 26 pages.
Visualizer: page grid of 106 heap pages; Segmented VACUUM / VACUUM FULL; Stepper through phases with dead-TID store bar, index panels, VM bits, FSM.
Playground: `orders` fillfactor 70; presets: stats, pg_visibility, vacuum + check, freespace, VACUUM FULL relfilenode.
Production: SaaS audit table bloat; DELETE + VACUUM + partitioning or pg_repack instead of nightly FULL.
Pitfalls: VACUUM FULL in business hours, long transactions block cleanup, expecting space back.

title: 4. autovacuum-tuning — Tuning autovacuum
text:
Facts: thresholds `50 + 0.2·reltuples` capped at `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` 100 M (new in 18); insert trigger `1000 + 0.2·reltuples·(1 − relallfrozen/relpages)`; analyze `50 + 0.1·reltuples`; naptime 1 min; 3 workers (`autovacuum_worker_slots` 16 in 18); cost delay 2 ms, limit 200 (from vacuum_cost_limit), page hit 1 / miss 2 / dirty 20; cost limit shared among workers; per-table storage parameters; autovacuum cancels on conflicting lock except anti-wraparound; no auto-ANALYZE of partitioned parents; stats from `track_counts` (routine-vacuuming.html, runtime-config-vacuum.html, runtime-config-autovacuum.html).
Visualizer: calculator (reltuples log slider, scale/threshold/cap, insert params, frozen %) + 24 h simulation of dead tuples with sawtooth autovacuum runs + cost-throttle MB/s.
Playground: `sessions` table with stats; presets compute the trigger from `pg_stat_user_tables` and `pg_class`, per-table reloptions, show settings.
Pitfalls: big tables never vacuumed under 0.2; disabled autovacuum; long transactions; frequent lock conflicts.

section: 5. xid-wraparound — XID wraparound, freezing and MultiXacts
title: 5. xid-wraparound — XID wraparound, freezing and MultiXacts
text:
Facts: 32-bit XIDs compared modulo 2^32 (2 B past / 2 B future); special XIDs 0/1/2; freezing sets a flag; `vacuum_freeze_min_age` 50 M; `vacuum_freeze_table_age` 150 M (≤ 95% of max); `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` 200 M (runs even if autovacuum off, not cancelled); failsafe 1.6 B; warnings 40 M before wrap, stop at 3 M; `relfrozenxid`/`datfrozenxid`; multixacts in xmax, 400 M max age, members area 10 GB/20 GB; recovery steps (no single-user mode, no VACUUM FULL/FREEZE) (routine-vacuuming.html, runtime-config-vacuum.html, transaction-id.html).
Visualizer: XID ring with current XID, relfrozenxid, horizon; slider for age; thresholds bands; toggle "frozen" tuple; "no freezing" mode showing a row vanish at age 2^31.
Playground: burn procedure (100k xids ≈ 0.2 s), age(relfrozenxid), VACUUM FREEZE, pg_visibility all_frozen, mxid_age.

title: 6. streaming-replication — Physical streaming replication
text:
Facts: walsender/walreceiver, `primary_conninfo`, `standby.signal`, hot standby read-only, slots retain WAL (`max_slot_wal_keep_size` -1), `wal_keep_size`, `synchronous_standby_names` FIRST/ANY, remote_write/on/remote_apply, lag columns sent/write/flush/replay, `max_standby_streaming_delay` 30 s, `hot_standby_feedback`, `pg_promote`, `pg_rewind` (warm-standby.html, hot-standby.html, monitoring-stats.html, runtime-config-replication.html, app-pgrewind.html).
Visualizer: live simulation primary → network → standby with sent/write/flush/replay pointers, sync mode Segmented, commit button, latency + replay-pause controls, disconnect → slot retained WAL grows.
Playground: physical slot, retained bytes, pg_stat_replication shape, pg_is_in_recovery, settings.

title: 7. logical-replication — Logical replication
text:
Facts: publication/subscription, pgoutput, replica identity (default PK, FULL, NOTHING → UPDATE/DELETE error), row filters + UPDATE transformation table, column lists, initial sync by table-sync workers, decoding in commit order, rolled-back never decoded, conflicts (insert_exists …) and SKIP, no DDL/sequences, 18 publishes stored generated columns (logical-replication*.html, logicaldecoding*.html).
Visualizer: Stepper of three interleaved transactions through reorder buffer → pgoutput filter → subscriber; interactive row-filter transformation table.
Playground: publications with row filter/column list, pg_publication_tables, replica identity catalog, `pg_logical_emit_message` visible in pg_walinspect.

title: 8. partitioning — Declarative partitioning and pruning
text:
Facts: range/list/hash; range upper bound exclusive; default partition; pruning at plan time / executor init (Subplans Removed) / run time (never executed); `enable_partition_pruning`; ATTACH (SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE) with pre-built CHECK; DETACH CONCURRENTLY (not with a default partition — measured); unique keys must include partition key; partition-wise join/aggregate off by default; DROP vs DELETE (ddl-partitioning.html, runtime-config-query.html).
Measured: DELETE one month = 1224 kB WAL, DROP partition = 4872 B.
Visualizer: query picker with real EXPLAIN output, partitions lit/pruned per stage, tuple routing.

title: 9. backup-pitr — Backups and point-in-time recovery
text:

text:
Facts: one process per connection, `max_connections` 100, `superuser_reserved_connections` 3, idle-in-transaction holds snapshot, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, `idle_session_timeout` warning about poolers, `transaction_timeout`, DISCARD ALL; PgBouncer modes (session/transaction/statement) are third-party behaviour (runtime-config-connection.html, runtime-config-client.html, sql-discard.html).

# Slice A — Preface, Part I Tutorial, Part II ch.4-7 (SQL Syntax, Data Definition, Data Manipulation, Queries)

Source: PostgreSQL 18.7 docs, `_order.tsv` idx 0-65 (66 pages). All pages read in full.

title: What PostgreSQL is, history, doc structure  [M1]
text:
- PostgreSQL is an **object-relational database management system (ORDBMS)** based on POSTGRES, Version 4.2, developed at UC Berkeley Computer Science Department. Open-source descendant of the Berkeley code.
- Headline features listed: complex queries, foreign keys, triggers, updatable views, transactional integrity, multiversion concurrency control (MVCC).
- User-extensible in: data types, functions, operators, aggregate functions, index methods, procedural languages.
- License: "liberal license" — usable/modifiable/distributable by anyone free of charge for any purpose (private, commercial, academic).
- History timeline:
  1. POSTGRES project led by Prof. Michael Stonebraker; sponsored by DARPA, ARO, NSF, ESL Inc. Implementation began **1986**.
  2. First "demoware" operational 1987, shown at 1988 ACM-SIGMOD. Version 1 released June 1989; Version 2 June 1990 (redesigned rule system); Version 3 in 1991 (multiple storage managers, improved executor, rewritten rule system).
  3. Late 1992: primary data manager for Sequoia 2000. Illustra (later Informix, now IBM) commercialized it. Berkeley project officially ended with **Version 4.2**.
  4. **1994**: Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen added an SQL interpreter -> **Postgres95**. Completely ANSI C, code size trimmed 25%, 30-50% faster on Wisconsin Benchmark vs POSTGRES 4.2. PostQUEL replaced by SQL (libpq is named after PostQUEL). Subqueries not supported until PostgreSQL. New `psql` (GNU Readline) replaced the old `monitor` program. libpgtcl added. Instance-level rule system removed (rewrite rules kept). GNU make used.
  5. **1996**: renamed **PostgreSQL**; version numbering restarted at **6.0**. "Postgres" remains an official project name/nickname.
- Documentation parts: I Tutorial; II The SQL Language; III Server Administration; IV Client Interfaces; V Server Programming; VI Reference; VII Internals; Appendices A-O (A Error Codes, B Date/Time Support, C SQL Key Words, D SQL Conformance, E Release Notes, F Additional Supplied Modules and Extensions, G Additional Supplied Programs, H External Projects, I Source Code Repository, J Documentation, K PostgreSQL Limits, L Acronyms, M Glossary, N Color Support, O Obsolete or Renamed Features).
- Part III chapters 16-31, Part IV 32-35 (libpq, Large Objects, ECPG, Information Schema), Part V 36-50 (Extending SQL, Triggers, Event Triggers, Rule System, Procedural Languages, PL/pgSQL, PL/Tcl, PL/Perl, PL/Python, SPI, Background Workers, Logical Decoding, Replication Progress Tracking, Archive Modules, OAuth Validator Modules), Part VII starts at ch.51 (Overview of Internals), 52 System Catalogs, 53 System Views, 54 Frontend/Backend Protocol, 55 Coding Conventions.
- Synopsis conventions: `[ ]` optional; `{ }` with `|` = choose one alternative; `...` = preceding element can repeat; everything else (including parentheses) literal. SQL prompt `=>`, shell prompt `$`.
- "Administrator" = person in charge of installing/running the server; "user" = anyone using any part of the system.

title: Bug reporting  [M1, low relevance]
text:
- A bug = program terminates with fatal signal / OS error pointing to the program; wrong output; refuses valid input; accepts invalid input without notice; fails to build per instructions on supported platforms. Slowness and non-conformance to SQL (unless claimed) are not necessarily bugs.
- Report must contain: exact reproducible steps from program start (self-contained: CREATE TABLE + INSERT + query; ideally a psql script, with empty `~/.psqlrc`); output received (most verbose: psql `\set VERBOSITY verbose`, server `log_error_verbosity = verbose`); expected output; changed options/env/config; deviations from install instructions; version (`SELECT version();`, `postgres --version`, `psql --version`); platform (kernel, C library, CPU, memory).
- Terminology: a single **backend process** crash differs from a crash of the parent "postgres" process; say which. psql (client) is separate from the backend.
- Where: `pgsql-bugs@lists.postgresql.org` (or web form); security issues privately to `security@postgresql.org`; docs issues to `pgsql-docs@lists.postgresql.org`; portability on unsupported platforms to `pgsql-hackers`. Not to user lists (pgsql-sql, pgsql-general).

title: Client/server architecture & getting connected  [M1]
text:
- PostgreSQL can be installed by any unprivileged user; no root needed.
- Environment variables: `PGHOST` (server host), `PGPORT` (port), `PGUSER` (role name; or `-U` switch).
- **Client/server model**. A session consists of cooperating processes:
  - A **server process** that manages database files, accepts connections, performs actions on behalf of clients. The server program is called **`postgres`**.
  - The user's **client (frontend) application**: text tool, GUI, web server, maintenance tool.
- Client and server can be on different hosts, communicating over TCP/IP; files accessible on the client may not be accessible (or have a different name) on the server.
- Concurrency model: the server "**forks**" a **new process for each connection**. From then on client and the new server process communicate without intervention by the original `postgres` process. The **supervisor server process** is always running, waiting for connections; client and associated server processes come and go.
- `createdb mydb` / `dropdb mydb` (shell wrappers). Default Unix socket path shown in error: `/tmp/.s.PGSQL.5432` (default port 5432).
- Typical failures and meaning:
  - `createdb: command not found` -> not installed / PATH (try `/usr/local/pgsql/bin/createdb`).
  - `connection to server on socket "/tmp/.s.PGSQL.5432" failed: No such file or directory` -> server not started or not listening there.
  - `FATAL: role "joe" does not exist` -> no PostgreSQL role for that OS user. PostgreSQL user accounts are distinct from OS accounts.
  - `ERROR: permission denied to create database` -> role lacks the privilege to create databases.
- There is always a PostgreSQL user with the same name as the OS user that started the server, and that user always has permission to create databases.
- Database names: must have an **alphabetic first character**, limited to **63 bytes**. `createdb` with no arg creates a DB named after the current user; many tools default the DB name to the user name. `dropdb` always needs an explicit name; it physically removes all files and cannot be undone.
- Access methods: psql; GUI tools (pgAdmin, ODBC/JDBC suites); custom apps via language bindings (Part IV).
- psql prompt `mydb=>` (ordinary user) vs `mydb=#` (**superuser** — not subject to access controls). Greeting `psql (18.7)`. `SELECT version();` returns e.g. `PostgreSQL 18.7 on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu, compiled by gcc ..., 64-bit`. `SELECT current_date;` `SELECT 2 + 2;` (column named `?column?`).
- psql internal (backslash) commands are not SQL: `\h` (SQL syntax help), `\?` (internal command help), `\q` (quit), `\i file` (run file); `psql -s` = single-step mode (pauses before sending each statement).

title: Relational concepts & first tables  [M1, M3]
text:
- PostgreSQL is a **relational DBMS**: manages data in **relations** (mathematical term for table). Contrast: hierarchical DB (Unix files/directories), object-oriented DB.
- Each **table** = named collection of **rows**; each row has the same set of named **columns**; each column has a **data type**. Columns have a fixed order; **SQL does not guarantee row order** in any way.
- Tables are grouped into **databases**; the collection of databases managed by a single server instance = **database cluster**.
- Tutorial sample files: source tree `src/tutorial/` (`make`, then `psql -s mydb`, `\i basics.sql`; ch.3 uses `advanced.sql`).
- Sample schema used throughout tutorial:
  ```sql
  CREATE TABLE weather (city varchar(80), temp_lo int, temp_hi int, prcp real, date date);
  CREATE TABLE cities (name varchar(80), location point);
  ```
- Lexical basics: whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) free-form; `--` comment to end of line; SQL is case-insensitive for key words and identifiers except double-quoted identifiers.
- Standard SQL types supported: `int`, `smallint`, `real`, `double precision`, `char`, `varchar`, `date`, `time`, `timestamp`, `interval`; plus general-utility and geometric types (`point` is PostgreSQL-specific). Type names are **not key words** in the syntax except where required for SQL-standard special cases (because users can define arbitrary types).
- `INSERT INTO weather VALUES ('San Francisco', 46, 50, 0.25, '1994-11-27');` — non-numeric constants in single quotes. `point` input: `'(-194.0, 53.0)'`.
- Column-list INSERT lets you reorder/omit columns (omitted -> default/NULL). Explicit column lists considered better style.
- `COPY weather FROM '/home/user/weather.txt';` — file must be on the **server (backend) machine**, since the backend reads it directly. Text format: tab-separated, `\N` = NULL. COPY is faster than INSERT but less flexible.
- `DROP TABLE tablename;`

title: Tutorial querying: SELECT, joins, aggregates, UPDATE, DELETE  [M3]
text:
- SELECT anatomy: **select list** (columns/expressions to return), **table list** (FROM), optional **qualification** (WHERE). `*` = all columns (bad style in production: adding a column changes results).
- Expressions in select list: `SELECT city, (temp_hi+temp_lo)/2 AS temp_avg, date FROM weather;` AS optional.
- WHERE takes a Boolean expression; only rows where it is **true** are returned; `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`.
- `ORDER BY city, temp_lo` — partial sort keys give unspecified order among ties.
- `SELECT DISTINCT city FROM weather;` — DISTINCT does **not** guarantee ordering in current PostgreSQL (older versions' implementation sorted as a side effect). Use `DISTINCT ... ORDER BY`.
- Join = query accessing multiple tables (or multiple instances of the same table) at once. Conceptual model: compare each pair of rows (actual execution is more efficient, invisible to user).
  - `SELECT * FROM weather JOIN cities ON city = name;` -> inner join; unmatched rows (Hayward) dropped; both join columns appear.
  - Qualify columns (`weather.city`) when names are ambiguous; good style to qualify all in joins.
  - Older implicit syntax `FROM weather, cities WHERE city = name` gives identical results; `JOIN/ON` was introduced in SQL-92.
  - `LEFT OUTER JOIN`: every left row appears at least once; unmatched right columns are NULL. Right outer and full outer joins also exist.
  - **Self join** with aliases: `FROM weather w1 JOIN weather w2 ON w1.temp_lo < w2.temp_lo AND w1.temp_hi > w2.temp_hi`.
- Aggregates: `count`, `sum`, `avg`, `max`, `min` compute one result from many rows.
  - Aggregates cannot appear in WHERE (WHERE determines which rows enter aggregation, so it is evaluated first). Use a subquery: `WHERE temp_lo = (SELECT max(temp_lo) FROM weather)`.
  - `GROUP BY city` -> one output row per group; `HAVING max(temp_lo) < 40` filters groups.
  - **WHERE vs HAVING**: WHERE selects input rows *before* grouping/aggregation (no aggregates allowed); HAVING selects group rows *after*. HAVING without aggregates is allowed but is better as WHERE (more efficient: avoids grouping rows that fail).
  - `FILTER`: per-aggregate row filter: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE temp_lo < 45)`; other aggregates in the same query still see all rows.
  - `LIKE 'S%'` pattern matching.
- `UPDATE weather SET temp_hi = temp_hi - 2, temp_lo = temp_lo - 2 WHERE date > '1994-11-28';`
- `DELETE FROM weather WHERE city = 'Hayward';` `DELETE FROM tablename;` with no qualification removes all rows — **no confirmation requested**.

title: Tutorial advanced: views, FKs, transactions, savepoints  [M3, M5, M6]
text:
- View = named query usable like a table: `CREATE VIEW myview AS SELECT name, temp_lo, temp_hi, prcp, date, location FROM weather, cities WHERE city = name;` Views encapsulate table structure behind consistent interfaces; views on views are common.
- Referential integrity via FK:
  ```sql
  CREATE TABLE cities (name varchar(80) primary key, location point);
  CREATE TABLE weather (city varchar(80) references cities(name), temp_lo int, temp_hi int, prcp real, date date);
  ```
  Violation message: `ERROR: insert or update on table "weather" violates foreign key constraint "weather_city_fkey"` / `DETAIL: Key (city)=(Berkeley) is not present in table "cities".` (auto constraint name pattern `<table>_<col>_fkey`).
- **Transaction** = bundles multiple steps into a single all-or-nothing operation. Properties described:
  - **Atomic**: from other transactions' viewpoint it happens completely or not at all.
  - **Durable**: all updates are logged in permanent storage (on disk) *before* the transaction is reported complete.
  - **Isolated**: updates by an open transaction are invisible to others until it completes, then all become visible simultaneously.
- `BEGIN; ... COMMIT;` = **transaction block**. `ROLLBACK` cancels. Without BEGIN, **every statement runs in its own implicit transaction** (implicit BEGIN and, if successful, COMMIT). Some client libraries issue BEGIN/COMMIT automatically.
- **Savepoints**: `SAVEPOINT name;` ... `ROLLBACK TO name;` discards changes after the savepoint, keeps earlier ones. After rolling back to a savepoint it **remains defined** (can roll back to it repeatedly). Releasing or rolling back to a savepoint **automatically releases all savepoints defined after it**. Releasing frees resources.
- `ROLLBACK TO` is the **only way to regain control of a transaction block put into aborted state by an error**, short of full rollback.
- Bank example: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100.00 WHERE name = 'Alice'; SAVEPOINT my_savepoint; UPDATE ... 'Bob'; ROLLBACK TO my_savepoint; UPDATE ... 'Wally'; COMMIT;`

title: Window functions (tutorial level)  [M3]
text:
- A window function computes across a set of rows related to the current row, **without collapsing rows** (unlike non-window aggregates).
- Always has an `OVER` clause directly after the function name/args — this is what syntactically distinguishes it. `PARTITION BY` divides rows into partitions; function computed across the current row's partition. `ORDER BY` inside OVER controls processing order (need not match output order).
- Example table `empsalary(depname, empno, salary, enroll_date)`; `avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY depname)`; `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC)` (ties numbered in unspecified order).
- Rows considered = the "virtual table" from FROM as filtered by WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING. Multiple window functions with different OVERs all act on that same row collection.
- Omit PARTITION BY -> single partition containing all rows.
- **Window frame**: per-row subset of its partition. Default frame: with ORDER BY = start of partition through current row **plus following peers equal per ORDER BY**; without ORDER BY = whole partition.
  - `sum(salary) OVER ()` -> same grand total (47100) on every row.
  - `sum(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary)` -> running sum where duplicates (4800, 4800; 5200, 5200) get the same value (25700; 41100) because peers are included.
- Allowed **only in SELECT list and ORDER BY**. Forbidden in GROUP BY, HAVING, WHERE — they logically execute after those. Window functions execute **after non-window aggregates**: an aggregate call may appear inside a window function's arguments, not vice versa.
- To filter on window results use a sub-select: `SELECT ... FROM (SELECT ..., row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC, empno) AS pos FROM empsalary) AS ss WHERE pos < 3;`
- Named windows: `SELECT sum(salary) OVER w, avg(salary) OVER w FROM empsalary WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC);`

title: Lexical structure  [M3, M4 (parser)]
text:
- SQL input = sequence of **commands**; a command = sequence of **tokens** terminated by `;` (end of input also terminates). Token kinds: key word, identifier, quoted identifier, literal/constant, special character symbol. Comments are not tokens (equivalent to whitespace).
- **Identifiers / key words**: begin with a letter (a-z, also letters with diacritics and non-Latin letters) or underscore; subsequent chars letters, underscores, digits 0-9, or `$` (dollar not allowed by SQL standard). The standard will never define a key word containing digits or starting/ending with underscore.
- Max identifier length: system uses at most **NAMEDATALEN-1 bytes**; default **NAMEDATALEN = 64** -> **63 bytes**; longer names are **truncated** (not an error). Change via `NAMEDATALEN` in `src/include/pg_config_manual.h`.
- Key words and unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive; unquoted names are **folded to lower case** (contrary to SQL standard, which folds to upper case). `FOO`, `foo`, `"foo"` are the same; `"Foo"` and `"FOO"` differ. Advice: always quote a name or never quote it.
- **Quoted (delimited) identifier**: `"..."`; always an identifier, never a key word; any char except code zero; embed `"` by doubling; length limit still applies; case-sensitive.
- Unicode-escaped identifier: `U&"d\0061t\+000061"` (4-hex-digit `\XXXX` or 6-hex-digit `\+XXXXXX`); custom escape char via `UESCAPE '!'` (any single char except hex digit, `+`, `'`, `"`, whitespace); double the escape char for a literal. Surrogate pairs accepted and combined. If server encoding is not UTF-8, code point is converted (error if impossible). `U&` conflicts with `&` operator — use spaces.
- **Constants**: three implicitly typed kinds: strings, bit strings, numbers.
  - String: `'...'`; embed quote by doubling (`'Dianne''s horse'`). Two string constants separated only by whitespace **containing at least one newline** are concatenated (`'foo'<newline>'bar'` = `'foobar'`); on the same line it is a syntax error (SQL standard behavior).
  - Escape string: `E'...'` (PostgreSQL extension). Table 4.1 escapes: `\b` backspace, `\f` form feed, `\n` newline, `\r` carriage return, `\t` tab, `\o`/`\oo`/`\ooo` octal byte, `\xh`/`\xhh` hex byte, `\uxxxx` / `\Uxxxxxxxx` 16/32-bit Unicode. Any other char after backslash taken literally (`\\`, `\'`). You are responsible for valid byte sequences in server encoding. Code-zero char cannot be in a string constant.
  - GUC **`standard_conforming_strings`**: default **on** since 9.1 -> backslashes are literal in ordinary strings, escapes only in `E''`. If off, backslash escapes recognized in both. Related GUCs: **`escape_string_warning`**, **`backslash_quote`**.
  - Unicode string: `U&'d\0061t\+000061'` [`UESCAPE '!'`]; only works when `standard_conforming_strings` is on (else rejected with error, for SQL-injection safety).
  - **Dollar quoting**: `$$...$$` or `$tag$...$tag$`; no escapes at all inside; nest by using different tags; tag follows unquoted-identifier rules but cannot contain `$`; tags are **case sensitive**; must be separated by whitespace from a preceding keyword/identifier. Not SQL standard. Classic use: function bodies (`$function$ ... $q$[\t\r\n\v\\]$q$ ... $function$`).
  - Bit string: `B'1001'` (only 0/1); hex `X'1FF'` (4 bits per hex digit). Continuable across lines like strings; no dollar quoting.
  - Numeric forms: `digits`, `digits.[digits][e[+-]digits]`, `[digits].digits[e[+-]digits]`, `digitse[+-]digits`. Non-decimal integers: `0xhex`, `0ooct`, `0bbin` (prefix and digits case-insensitive; integers only). Underscores for grouping between digits: `1_500_000_000`, `0b10001000_00000000`, `0o_1_755`, `0xFFFF_FFFF`, `1.618_034`; not at start/end of constant or digit group (not adjacent to decimal point or exponent marker), no double underscore. A leading `+`/`-` is an **operator**, not part of the constant.
  - **Initial type of numeric constant**: no decimal point/exponent -> `integer` if fits 32 bits, else `bigint` if fits 64 bits, else `numeric`. With decimal point and/or exponent -> always `numeric`. Then coerced by type resolution.
  - Typed constants: `type 'string'`, `'string'::type`, `CAST('string' AS type)`; also `typename('string')` for some types. `type 'string'` works only for simple literal constants and **not for array types**. `CAST` is SQL standard; `type 'string'` is a generalization of standard; `::` and function-call are historical PostgreSQL.
- **Operators**: name = up to NAMEDATALEN-1 (63) chars from `+ - * / < > = ~ ! @ # % ^ & | \` ?`. Restrictions: `--` and `/*` cannot appear in an operator name; a multi-char operator cannot end in `+` or `-` unless it also contains one of `~ ! @ # % ^ & | \` ?` (so `@-` OK, `*-` not).
- **Special characters**: `$n` positional parameter; `()` grouping/precedence; `[]` array element; `,` list separator; `;` terminates command; `:` array slice (and variable prefix in Embedded SQL); `*` all fields / parameterless aggregate; `.` numeric constants and schema.table.column separator.
- **Comments**: `-- to end of line`; `/* ... */` block comments **nest** (per SQL standard, unlike C). Removed before syntax analysis, replaced by whitespace.
- **Operator precedence (Table 4.2, highest to lowest)**:

  | Operator/Element | Assoc. | Description |
  |---|---|---|
  | `.` | left | table/column name separator |
  | `::` | left | PostgreSQL-style typecast |
  | `[ ]` | left | array element selection |
  | `+ -` | right | unary plus, unary minus |
  | `COLLATE` | left | collation selection |
  | `AT` | left | AT TIME ZONE, AT LOCAL |
  | `^` | left | exponentiation |
  | `* / %` | left | multiplication, division, modulo |
  | `+ -` | left | addition, subtraction |
  | (any other operator) | left | all other native and user-defined operators |
  | `BETWEEN IN LIKE ILIKE SIMILAR` | — | range containment, set membership, string matching |
  | `< > = <= >= <>` | — | comparison operators |
  | `IS ISNULL NOTNULL` | — | IS TRUE, IS FALSE, IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM, etc. |
  | `NOT` | right | logical negation |
  | `AND` | left | logical conjunction |
  | `OR` | left | logical disjunction |

  - Precedence is **hard-wired into the parser**; applies to user-defined operators with the same names as built-ins. `OPERATOR(schema.op)` always has "any other operator" precedence regardless of which operator is inside. Note `^` is left-associative. Pre-9.5 rules differed (`<= >= <>` were generic operators; IS tests had higher priority).

title: Value expressions  [M3, M4]
text:
- Kinds: constant; column reference; positional parameter; subscripted expr; field selection; operator invocation; function call; aggregate expression; window function call; type cast; collation expression; scalar subquery; array constructor; row constructor; parenthesized expression. Plus special constructs (e.g. `IS NULL`) documented in ch.9.
- Column reference: `correlation.columnname` (correlation = table name, possibly schema-qualified, or FROM alias); qualifier optional if unique.
- Positional parameter: `$number` (SQL function bodies, prepared statements, out-of-line client parameters).
- Subscripts: `expression[subscript]`, slice `expression[lower:upper]`; subscript expressions are **rounded to nearest integer**; parenthesize the array expression unless it is a column reference or positional parameter: `(arrayfunction(a,b))[42]`, `mytable.two_d_column[17][34]`, `$1[10:42]`.
- Field selection: `expression.fieldname`; parentheses required for composite columns: `(compositecol).somefield`, `(mytable.compositecol).somefield`, `(rowfunction(a,b)).col3`; `(compositecol).*` for all fields. A qualified column reference is a special case of field selection.
- Operator invocation: `expr op expr` (binary infix), `op expr` (unary prefix) — no postfix operators; `OPERATOR(schema.operatorname)`.
- Function call: `function_name([expression [, ...]])`. Functional/attribute notation interchangeable for single composite arg: `col(table)` == `table.col` ("computed fields").
- **Aggregate expression syntax** (5 forms):
  ```
  aggregate_name (expression [ , ... ] [ order_by_clause ] ) [ FILTER ( WHERE filter_clause ) ]
  aggregate_name (ALL expression [ , ... ] [ order_by_clause ] ) [ FILTER ( WHERE filter_clause ) ]
  aggregate_name (DISTINCT expression [ , ... ] [ order_by_clause ] ) [ FILTER ( WHERE filter_clause ) ]
  aggregate_name ( * ) [ FILTER ( WHERE filter_clause ) ]
  aggregate_name ( [ expression [ , ... ] ] ) WITHIN GROUP ( order_by_clause ) [ FILTER ( WHERE filter_clause ) ]
  ```
  - ALL is default. DISTINCT: once per distinct value (or distinct set for multiple exprs). `(*)`: once per input row (only useful for `count(*)`).
  - Most aggregates **ignore null inputs** (all built-ins unless stated). `count(*)` = total rows; `count(f1)` = non-null f1; `count(distinct f1)` = distinct non-null.
  - Input order is unspecified unless `ORDER BY` inside the argument list (after all args): `array_agg(v ORDER BY v DESC)`, `string_agg(a, ',' ORDER BY a)`. Aggregate ORDER BY expressions cannot be output-column names/numbers. `string_agg(a ORDER BY a, ',')` is syntactically valid but wrong (one arg, two sort keys).
  - jsonb keeps the last matching key, so ordering matters: `jsonb_object_agg(k, v ORDER BY v)`.
  - With DISTINCT + ORDER BY, ORDER BY expressions can only reference columns in the DISTINCT list.
  - **Ordered-set aggregates** require `WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...)`; args before WITHIN GROUP are **direct arguments** (evaluated once per aggregate call, not per row; may contain variables only if grouped); empty direct-arg list written `()` (PostgreSQL also accepts `(*)`). Example: `percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY income)`.
  - `FILTER (WHERE ...)`: only rows where filter is true are fed.
  - Aggregate may appear only in the **result list or HAVING** of a SELECT. In a subquery, if the aggregate's arguments (and filter) contain only outer-level variables, the aggregate **belongs to the nearest such outer level** and acts as an outer reference/constant for the subquery.
- **Window function call syntax**:
